games.title: Torque or force?
items: In a uniform field a dipole feels zero net force.
qE and -qE cancel.
In a uniform field the torque on a dipole is always zero.
τ = pE sinθ is zero only at θ = 0° or 180°.
The torque on a dipole tends to align p along E.
That is the stable direction.
A neutral paper bit is attracted by a charged comb because the comb's field is uniform.
Attraction needs a non-uniform field.
A non-polar molecule can acquire an induced dipole moment in an electric field.
The field pushes its positive and negative charge centres apart.

quiz.q: A dipole with p = 2 × 10⁻⁸ C m is placed at 90° to a uniform field of 10⁵ N C⁻¹. What is the torque (in mN m)?
What is the net force on an electric dipole placed in a uniform electric field?
quiz.explain: The charges feel qE and -qE, which are equal and opposite.
steps: In a uniform field +q feels qE and −q feels −qE
These are equal and opposite, so they cancel
quiz.mistake: Adds the forces instead of noting they are opposite

quiz.q: A dipole of moment 3 × 10⁻⁹ C m is at 30° to a field of 2 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹. What is the torque (in units of 10⁻⁵ N m)?
Which of these molecules has a permanent electric dipole moment?
quiz.explain: Water's bent shape puts its charge centres apart, so it is polar. CO₂ is linear and symmetric, so its moments cancel.
steps: Water is bent, so its charge centres are separated: permanent dipole
O₂ and H₂ are symmetric; linear CO₂'s bond moments cancel
quiz.mistake: Thinks any molecule with polar bonds is polar overall

quiz.q: Why does a charged comb attract small bits of neutral paper?
options: The comb's field is uniform, giving a net force
It polarises the paper and the non-uniform field pulls the induced dipoles towards it
Gravity is reduced near the comb
quiz.explain: Induced dipoles in a non-uniform field feel a net force towards the stronger field near the comb.
steps: The comb's field polarises the neutral paper (induced dipoles)
The comb's field is non-uniform, so the dipoles feel a net force towards stronger field
Answer: It polarises the paper and the non-uniform field pulls the induced dipoles towards it
quiz.mistake: Thinks only charged objects can be attracted

quiz.q: The torque on a dipole in a uniform field is maximum when the angle between p and E is
quiz.explain: sin θ is largest at 90°.
quiz.mistake: Confuses torque with potential energy, which is extreme at 0° and 180°

quiz.q: An ideal electric dipole is one in which
options: the charges are equal to 1 C
the charges become infinite and the separation tends to zero, keeping p finite
the dipole has a net positive charge
quiz.explain: This limit gives a point dipole whose field formulas are exact at all r.
steps: The product p = q × 2a stays finite
Answer: the charges become infinite and the separation tends to zero, keeping p finite
quiz.mistake: Thinks ideal means a particular value of charge

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A dipole in a uniform field may rotate but does not move bodily. Reason (R): The two forces on it are equal and opposite but do not act along the same line. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Equal and opposite forces with different lines of action form a couple: zero net force but non-zero torque.
steps: A: a dipole in a uniform field rotates but does not move bodily – true
R: the forces are equal and opposite but not along the same line – true
Such a couple gives zero net force but non-zero torque, so R explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Does not connect a couple with rotation without translation

teach.ask: Gappu sees a paper bit jump to a charged comb. 'But paper is neutral! How?'
teach.praise: Chirp! The comb makes induced dipoles in the paper, and its non-uniform field pulls them. Neat!
teach.nudge: Good! What happens inside the neutral paper near the comb, and why does it matter that the field is not uniform?

revise.summary: In a uniform field a dipole feels zero net force but a torque τ = p × E (τ = pE sinθ) that aligns it with E. Polar molecules have permanent dipoles; non-polar ones get induced dipoles, and in non-uniform fields dipoles feel a net force.
focus: Net force and torque on a dipole
remember: τ = pE sinθ; maximum at 90°, zero at 0° and 180°
Polar: H₂O, HCl; non-polar: O₂, H₂, CO₂
traps: Zero net force does not mean zero torque
CO₂ is not polar: its bond moments cancel

learn.hook: Counting every electron on a charged wire is impossible. Instead, physicists use charge per metre, per square metre or per cubic metre, then let Gauss's law do the heavy lifting.
points: Linear charge density λ = charge per unit length (C m⁻¹), surface density σ = charge per unit area (C m⁻²), volume density ρ = charge per unit volume (C m⁻³).
For a continuous distribution, the total field is the integral (vector sum) of the fields of tiny elements: E = ∫ k dq r̂/r².
Charge is quantised, but over areas and volumes that hold billions of charges, averaging makes it look smooth, so densities make sense.
Gauss's law: the total electric flux through any closed surface = q_enclosed/ε₀.
Proof idea: for a charge q at the centre of a sphere of radius r, E = kq/r² everywhere on it, so flux = E × 4πr² = q/ε₀, the same for any radius or any closed shape enclosing q.

example.q: A point charge of 8.854 nC sits at the centre of a cube. What is the total flux through the cube? (ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²)
example.answer: 1000 N m² C⁻¹ (the cube's size does not matter)

learn.reallife: Engineers designing BHEL's high-voltage insulators estimate fields using charge densities and Gauss's law instead of tracking individual charges.

games.title: Density detective
pairs: Total flux through a closed surface

games.title: Gauss's law check
items: Gauss's law is true for any closed surface, whatever its shape.
Flux depends only on enclosed charge.
Flux through a sphere around a point charge increases with the sphere's radius.
E falls as 1/r² while area grows as r², so the flux stays q/ε₀.
Gauss's law contains only the charge enclosed by the surface.
Outside charges give zero net flux.
Charge densities make sense only because charge is not quantised.
Charge is quantised; densities work by averaging over huge numbers of charges.
The SI unit of linear charge density is C m⁻¹.
Charge per metre.

quiz.q: A thin rod 50 cm long carries a uniform charge of 2 µC. What is its linear charge density (in µC m⁻¹)?
quiz.explain: λ = q/L = 2 µC/0.5 m = 4 µC m⁻¹.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to convert cm to m

quiz.q: A charge of 17.708 nC lies inside a closed surface. What is the total flux through the surface (in N m² C⁻¹)? (ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²)
quiz.mistake: Slips by a factor of 10 with nano and pico

quiz.q: A point charge sits at the centre of a sphere. If the radius of the sphere is doubled, the total flux through it
quiz.explain: Flux = q/ε₀ depends only on the enclosed charge.
steps: It does not depend on the radius of the sphere
quiz.mistake: Thinks a bigger surface catches more flux

quiz.q: Gauss's law states that the total flux through a closed surface equals
options: the net charge enclosed multiplied by ε₀
the net charge enclosed divided by ε₀
the total charge inside and outside divided by ε₀
the field multiplied by the charge
quiz.explain: φ = q_enc/ε₀ for any closed surface.
steps: Gauss's law: total flux through a closed surface = q_enc/ε₀
Answer: the net charge enclosed divided by ε₀
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by ε₀ instead of dividing

quiz.q: A metal sheet of area 2 m² carries a uniform charge of 6 µC. What is its surface charge density (in µC m⁻²)?
quiz.explain: σ = q/A = 6/2 = 3 µC m⁻².

quiz.q: In the proof of Gauss's law for a point charge at the centre of a sphere, why is E·dS simply E dS everywhere?
options: The field is zero on the sphere
The field is radial, so it is along the outward normal at every point of the sphere
The field is parallel to the surface
quiz.explain: By symmetry E is radial and the sphere's normal is radial, so the angle between them is zero.
steps: By symmetry the field of a central charge is radial
The sphere's outward normal is also radial, so the angle is 0 and E·dS = E dS
Answer: The field is radial, so it is along the outward normal at every point of the sphere
quiz.mistake: Thinks the sphere must be a conductor

quiz.q: Why can we use smooth charge densities even though charge is quantised?
options: Small elements still contain huge numbers of charges, so averaging gives a smooth density
quiz.explain: Macroscopic averaging over regions large compared with atomic sizes hides the graininess.
steps: Even tiny elements of a body contain huge numbers of charges
Averaging over them hides the graininess, giving smooth densities
Answer: Small elements still contain huge numbers of charges, so averaging gives a smooth density

quiz.q: The field of a continuous charge distribution is found by
options: treating the whole body as a point charge at its edge
dividing it into small elements dq and adding their fields as vectors (integration)
adding only the charges at the surface
multiplying the density by the distance
quiz.explain: Superposition extends to continuous charge by integration.
steps: Split the body into small elements dq, each like a point charge
Add their fields as vectors: E = ∫ k dq r̂/r²
Answer: dividing it into small elements dq and adding their fields as vectors (integration)
quiz.mistake: Treats an extended body as a single point at any distance

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why does a bigger balloon around a charge not catch more flux?'
teach.praise: Chirp! The field weakens as 1/r² exactly as the area grows as r², so flux is just enclosed charge over ε₀!
teach.nudge: Nearly! What does the flux depend on, and why does the surface size not matter?

revise.summary: Continuous charge is described by λ, σ and ρ, and its field is the vector integral of element fields. Gauss's law says the total flux through any closed surface equals the enclosed charge divided by ε₀.
focus: Linear, surface and volume charge densities
Proof idea for a point charge
remember: λ = q/L, σ = q/A, ρ = q/V
Flux does not depend on the shape or size of the closed surface
traps: Charges outside do not add to net flux
Flux is q/ε₀, not qε₀

learn.hook: A charge sitting outside your Gaussian box is like a car driving straight through a toll plaza: it comes in one side and leaves the other, contributing nothing net.
points: A charge outside a closed surface sends as many lines in as out, so its net flux contribution is zero (though it still affects E at the surface).
Choose a Gaussian surface that matches the symmetry (sphere, cylinder, pillbox) so that E is constant and normal (or parallel) over each part.
A closed cube or cylinder in a uniform field has zero net flux: what enters one face leaves another.
Reverse use: if the flux through a closed surface is known from the field, the enclosed charge is q = ε₀φ.
A charge q at the centre of a cube sends q/6ε₀ through each face by symmetry.

example.q: A cube of side 0.1 m is in a field Ex = 50x N C⁻¹ (x in m), with faces at x = 0.1 m and x = 0.2 m. Find the net flux and the charge inside.
steps: Field is along x, so only the two faces normal to x carry flux.
example.answer: φ = 0.05 N m² C⁻¹ and q ≈ 4.4 × 10⁻¹³ C

learn.reallife: Signalling and data cables used by Indian Railways often have a metal sheath. Field lines from charges outside end on the sheath, so outside electric disturbances do not reach the wires inside.

games.title: Gaussian thinking
items: A charge just outside a closed surface contributes zero net flux through it.
Lines enter and leave.
If the net flux through a surface is zero, the field on the surface must be zero everywhere.
Only the net enclosed charge is zero; E can be non-zero.
A charge at the centre of a cube sends one sixth of its total flux through each face.
All six faces are symmetric.
A closed cylinder in a uniform field has zero net flux.
No charge is enclosed.
Gauss's law is useful only for spheres.
Any symmetric surface (cylinder, pillbox, sphere) can be used.

games.title: Net flux through the closed surface
items: Cube in a uniform field
Sphere with +q inside
Box with +q and -q inside
Sphere with +2q outside it
Cylinder with -q on its axis inside
Box with +3q and -q inside

quiz.q: A point charge of 6 µC is at the centre of a cube. What is the flux through one face, in terms of 1/ε₀ (in µC)?
quiz.explain: Total flux 6 µC/ε₀ divides equally among 6 faces: 1 µC/ε₀ each.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to share the flux among six faces

quiz.q: A closed cylinder lies with its axis along a uniform electric field. The net flux through it is
options: E times the area of one end
quiz.explain: Flux enters one end and leaves the other; the curved surface has no flux; no charge is enclosed.
steps: The field is uniform: flux in through one end = flux out through the other
Curved surface is parallel to E: no flux; no charge enclosed

quiz.q: The net outward flux through a closed box is 8000 N m² C⁻¹. What charge (in nC) is inside? (ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²; give to 2 decimal places)
quiz.mistake: Divides φ by ε₀ instead of multiplying

quiz.q: Charges +3 µC, -5 µC are inside a closed surface and +10 µC is outside. The net flux is (in µC/ε₀)
quiz.explain: Only enclosed charges count: 3 - 5 = -2 µC, so φ = -2 µC/ε₀.
steps: Gauss's law counts only enclosed charges
q_enc = +3 − 5 = −2 µC (the +10 µC outside does not count)

quiz.q: The net flux through a closed surface is zero. What can we conclude?
options: The net charge enclosed is zero
There is no charge anywhere nearby
The field on the surface is zero everywhere
The surface must be a sphere
quiz.explain: Zero flux means q_enc = 0; there may still be charges inside summing to zero, or charges outside.
steps: Charges may still exist inside (summing to zero) or outside
Answer: The net charge enclosed is zero
quiz.mistake: Concludes that E is zero on the surface

quiz.q: Why do we choose a cylindrical Gaussian surface for an infinitely long charged wire?
options: The wire's field is parallel to the curved surface
The field is radial and has the same magnitude at equal distances, matching a cylinder's symmetry
Spheres are not allowed for wires
quiz.explain: On the curved surface E is constant and along the normal; on the flat ends E is parallel to the surface, giving zero flux.
steps: A long wire's field is radial and equal at equal distances
A coaxial cylinder has E constant and normal on its curved face; ends give zero flux
Answer: The field is radial and has the same magnitude at equal distances, matching a cylinder's symmetry
quiz.mistake: Thinks any surface is equally convenient

quiz.q: A charge q is placed at one corner of a cube. What is the flux through the whole cube?
quiz.explain: Eight such cubes would surround the corner completely, so this cube gets one eighth of q/ε₀.
steps: Eight identical cubes meeting at that corner would enclose q fully
By symmetry each gets 1/8 of the total flux q/ε₀
quiz.mistake: Uses q/ε₀ without noticing only part of the charge's flux enters the cube

quiz.q: A field E = 3x î N C⁻¹ (x in m) exists. A cube of side 1 m has faces at x = 1 m and x = 2 m. What is the net flux through it (in N m² C⁻¹)?
quiz.explain: Out through x = 2: 6 × 1 = 6; in through x = 1: 3 × 1 = 3. Net = 6 - 3 = 3 N m² C⁻¹. Other faces are parallel to E.
quiz.mistake: Adds both faces or uses only one

teach.ask: Gappu put a charge outside his Gaussian box. 'Why is the flux zero if the field still pokes my box?'
teach.praise: Chirp! The outside charge's lines go in and come out, so only enclosed charge counts. Clever!
teach.nudge: Good thinking! What happens to each field line from an outside charge as it passes through the box?

revise.summary: Only enclosed charge contributes to net flux, so closed surfaces in uniform fields have zero flux. Gaussian surfaces are chosen to match symmetry, q = ε₀φ finds enclosed charge, and symmetry splits flux, e.g. q/6ε₀ per cube face.
focus: Flux from charges inside vs outside
remember: Charge at cube centre: q/6ε₀ per face; at a corner: q/8ε₀ through the cube
traps: Zero flux does not mean zero field on the surface
Don't count outside charges in q_enc

learn.hook: An overhead high-tension line is, to a nearby bird, almost an infinitely long charged wire. Gauss's law gives its field in two lines of algebra.
points: Infinitely long straight wire with uniform λ: Gaussian cylinder of radius r and length l gives E × 2πrl = λl/ε₀, so E = λ/(2πε₀r), radial and ∝ 1/r.
Infinite plane sheet with uniform σ: pillbox through the sheet gives 2EA = σA/ε₀, so E = σ/(2ε₀), normal to the sheet and independent of distance.
Two parallel plates with +σ and -σ: fields add between them to give σ/ε₀, and cancel outside to give zero.
These fields are directed away from positive charge and towards negative charge.
Real wires and sheets are finite, but the results hold well close to them and away from the edges.

example.q: An infinite line charge produces a field of 9 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹ at 2 cm. Find λ.

learn.reallife: Electrostatic precipitators at Indian thermal power plants (like those of NTPC) use a charged central wire inside a tube. The strong λ/(2πε₀r) field near the wire charges smoke particles so they collect on the walls.

items.text: The field of an infinite sheet is ___ of distance.
For a line charge, the field varies as 1/___.
For a line charge, the Gaussian surface is a ___.
Between two oppositely charged plates, E = σ/___.

quiz.q: A long straight wire has λ = 2 × 10⁻⁶ C m⁻¹. What is the field 10 cm from it (in N C⁻¹)? (1/4πε₀ = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
The field of an infinite line charge at 4 cm is 600 N C⁻¹. What is it at 12 cm (in N C⁻¹)?
quiz.explain: E ∝ 1/r for a line charge, so tripling r gives 600/3 = 200 N C⁻¹.
steps: r: 4 cm → 12 cm is 3 times larger
quiz.mistake: Uses 1/r² as for a point charge

quiz.q: An infinite plane sheet has σ = 17.708 × 10⁻¹² C m⁻². What is the field near it (in N C⁻¹)? (ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²)
quiz.mistake: Uses σ/ε₀, the result for a conductor or between plates

quiz.q: How does the field of an infinite plane sheet of charge change as you move away from it?
quiz.explain: E = σ/(2ε₀) has no r in it: the field lines are parallel.
steps: Field lines are parallel, so E stays constant
quiz.mistake: Applies a point-charge law to a sheet

quiz.q: Two large parallel plates carry σ = +8.854 × 10⁻¹² C m⁻² and -8.854 × 10⁻¹² C m⁻². What is the field between them (in N C⁻¹)?
quiz.explain: Between the plates E = σ/ε₀ = 1 N C⁻¹.
steps: Between oppositely charged plates the fields add: E = σ/ε₀
quiz.mistake: Uses σ/2ε₀ for one sheet only

quiz.q: For the same pair of oppositely charged plates, what is the field outside them?
quiz.explain: Outside, the two sheet fields are equal and opposite, so they cancel.
steps: Outside, the +σ and −σ sheet fields are equal (σ/2ε₀) and opposite
quiz.mistake: Thinks the field leaks outside equally

quiz.q: In deriving E for an infinite line charge, why is there no flux through the flat ends of the Gaussian cylinder?
options: The radial field is parallel to the end faces, so E·dS = 0 there
The field is zero at the ends
quiz.explain: E is radial (perpendicular to the wire) and the end faces' normals are along the wire.
steps: The field of a line charge is radial, perpendicular to the wire
The end faces' normals are along the wire, so E ⟂ normal and E·dS = 0
Answer: The radial field is parallel to the end faces, so E·dS = 0 there
quiz.mistake: Thinks the ends contribute because they are part of the surface

quiz.q: Two infinite parallel sheets both carry the same positive σ. What is the field between them?
quiz.explain: Each sheet gives σ/2ε₀ pointing away from itself. Between them these point in opposite directions and cancel.
steps: Each positive sheet gives σ/2ε₀ pointing away from itself
Between them the two fields point in opposite directions
quiz.mistake: Copies the result for oppositely charged plates

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why doesn't a giant charged sheet get weaker as I fly away from it?'
teach.praise: Chirp! The sheet's lines are parallel and never spread out, so E = σ/2ε₀ everywhere. Whoa!
teach.nudge: Almost! What do the field lines of a huge sheet look like, and why does that matter?

revise.summary: Gauss's law gives E = λ/(2πε₀r) for an infinite line charge and E = σ/(2ε₀) for an infinite sheet. Between oppositely charged parallel plates the field is σ/ε₀ and outside it is zero.
focus: Field of an infinite line charge
Field of an infinite plane sheet
remember: Sheet: E = σ/(2ε₀), independent of distance
Opposite plates: σ/ε₀ inside, 0 outside; like plates: 0 between
traps: Line field ∝ 1/r, not 1/r²
Sheet field is σ/2ε₀, not σ/ε₀

topics.title: Gauss's law: spherical shells and problem solving

learn.hook: Stand inside a hollow charged metal globe at a science fair and your hair stays flat. Gauss's law says the field inside is exactly zero.
points: Uniformly charged thin shell of radius R and charge q: outside (r > R) E = kq/r², as if all charge were at the centre.
Inside the shell (r < R) a Gaussian sphere encloses no charge, so E = 0 everywhere inside.
Just outside, E = kq/R² = σ/ε₀, where σ = q/4πR². The field jumps from 0 to σ/ε₀ across the shell.
Charge on a conductor from field: σ = ε₀E just outside, and q = σ × area.
Strategy: spot the symmetry, draw the Gaussian surface through the point, find q_enclosed, then solve for E.

example.q: A conducting sphere of radius 10 cm carries 1 nC. Find E at 5 cm and at 30 cm from the centre.

learn.reallife: Aircraft and Vande Bharat coaches act like metal shells: if lightning strikes, the charge stays on the outer skin and the field inside is close to zero, keeping passengers safe.

games.title: Shell secrets
items: The field inside a uniformly charged thin spherical shell is zero.
No charge is enclosed by a sphere drawn inside.
Outside a charged shell, the field is as if all charge were at its centre.
Gauss's law gives kq/r².
The field just inside a charged shell equals σ/ε₀.
It is zero inside; σ/ε₀ is just outside.
For r > R, the shell's field does not depend on R.
E = kq/r² contains only q and r.
The field inside a shell is zero only at its exact centre.
It is zero everywhere inside.

games.title: Gauss's law solution steps
games.prompt: Steps for finding E with Gauss's law
items: Identify the symmetry of the charge distribution
Choose a Gaussian surface through the point
Find the charge enclosed by the surface
Write flux = E × area where E is constant and normal
Solve E = q_enc/(ε₀ × area)

quiz.q: A thin shell of radius 20 cm carries 4 nC. What is the field at 10 cm from its centre (in N C⁻¹)?
quiz.explain: 10 cm is inside the shell, where q_enc = 0, so E = 0.
steps: r = 10 cm < R = 20 cm, so the point is inside the shell
A Gaussian sphere there encloses no charge

quiz.q: For the same shell (4 nC, radius 20 cm), what is the field at 60 cm from the centre (in N C⁻¹)?
quiz.mistake: Uses the shell radius instead of the distance from the centre

quiz.q: The field just outside a charged conductor is 8.854 × 10⁵ N C⁻¹. What is the surface charge density (in µC m⁻²)? (ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²)
A spherical conductor of radius 0.3 m has σ = 10⁻⁶ C m⁻². What is the field just outside it (in units of 10⁵ N C⁻¹)? (ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²; give to 2 decimal places)
quiz.explain: E = σ/ε₀ = 10⁻⁶/8.854 × 10⁻¹² ≈ 1.13 × 10⁵ N C⁻¹. The radius is not needed.
steps: Just outside a conductor: E = σ/ε₀ (radius not needed)

quiz.q: Which graph best describes E versus r for a charged thin spherical shell of radius R?
options: Rising linearly up to R then constant
Zero up to R, then a jump to a maximum at R, falling as 1/r² outside
Maximum at the centre, falling everywhere outward
quiz.explain: Inside E = 0; at R it jumps to kq/R²; outside it falls as 1/r².
steps: At r = R: jumps to kq/R²; outside: falls as 1/r²
Answer: Zero up to R, then a jump to a maximum at R, falling as 1/r² outside
quiz.mistake: Confuses the shell with a uniformly charged solid sphere

quiz.q: Why is the field outside a uniformly charged shell the same as that of a point charge at its centre?
options: A concentric Gaussian sphere outside encloses the full charge q and has the same symmetry as a point charge
Because the shell's charge moves to the centre
Because the shell is a conductor
Because the field inside is zero
quiz.explain: Gauss's law with spherical symmetry gives E·4πr² = q/ε₀ exactly as for a point charge.
steps: A concentric Gaussian sphere outside encloses all of q
Spherical symmetry gives E × 4πr² = q/ε₀, the point-charge result
Answer: A concentric Gaussian sphere outside encloses the full charge q and has the same symmetry as a point charge
quiz.mistake: Thinks charge physically moves to the centre

quiz.q: A charged shell's field at its outer surface is E₀. What is the field at a distance 2R from the centre?
quiz.explain: E ∝ 1/r² outside; going from R to 2R divides by 4.
steps: r: R → 2R, so E = E₀/2² = E₀/4

quiz.q: A thin plastic (insulating) spherical shell carries charge spread uniformly over it. A small charged bead is held at rest inside it, not touching. The force on the bead due to the shell's charge is
options: zero, because the field inside the shell is zero
directed towards the nearest point of the shell
quiz.explain: The uniformly spread charge on the shell produces no field anywhere inside it, so the bead feels no force from the shell.
steps: A Gaussian sphere inside the shell encloses none of the shell's charge
So the shell's field inside is zero and exerts no force on the bead
Answer: zero, because the field inside the shell is zero
quiz.mistake: Assumes the nearest part of the shell dominates

teach.ask: Gappu sits inside a charged hollow ball and asks: 'Why don't I feel any electric push?'
teach.praise: Chirp! A Gaussian sphere inside the shell encloses no charge, so the field is zero. I'm safe!
teach.nudge: Good! Draw a Gaussian sphere inside the shell. How much charge does it enclose?

revise.summary: For a uniformly charged thin shell, E = 0 inside and E = kq/r² outside, as if the charge were at the centre; just outside E = σ/ε₀. Use symmetry, a Gaussian surface and q_enc to solve problems.
focus: Field inside and outside a shell
remember: Just outside: E = σ/ε₀; σ = ε₀E
traps: Inside a shell the field is zero, not maximum
The radius is not needed for E = σ/ε₀

learn.hook: Lifting a bucket up a well stores energy that does not care which staircase you take. Electric forces behave the same way, which lets us define electric potential.
points: The electrostatic (Coulomb) force is conservative: the work it does depends only on the start and end points, not on the path.
So we can define electric potential energy U. Work done by an external force in moving a charge slowly (no change in kinetic energy) from P to R equals U(R) - U(P).
Only differences in U are physical; we usually choose U = 0 at infinity.
Electric potential V at a point = work done by an external force per unit positive test charge in bringing it slowly from infinity to that point: V = W/q.
Like height in a building, the zero of potential is a choice. Only potential differences can be measured and matter physically.

example.q: An external agent does 6 × 10⁻⁵ J of work to bring a charge of 2 µC slowly from infinity to point P. Find the potential at P.

learn.reallife: A Mumbai local train climbing from a station to a flyover gains the same potential energy whichever route it uses; charges in a circuit gain or lose energy in the same path-independent way.

games.title: Conservative or not?
items: The work done by the electrostatic force around a closed path is zero.
Conservative forces do zero work over closed loops.
Electric potential energy can be defined because Coulomb force is conservative.
Path independence makes U well defined.
The absolute value of potential at a point can be measured without choosing a reference.
Only differences are physical; a zero must be chosen.
Work done by the external agent in bringing a charge slowly equals the change in potential energy.
No kinetic energy is gained when moved slowly.
Work done by electrostatic force depends on the path taken.
It depends only on the end points.

items.text: V = W/___ (work per unit positive test charge).
Usually the potential is taken as zero at ___.
The Coulomb force is a ___ force.
Only potential ___ are physically meaningful.

quiz.q: An external force does 4 × 10⁻⁴ J of work to bring a 2 µC charge slowly from infinity to a point. What is the potential there (in V)?
Why can electric potential energy be defined for electrostatic forces?
options: Because the force is very strong
Because the electrostatic force is conservative
quiz.explain: A conservative force does path-independent work, so U depends only on position.
steps: U can be defined only if work depends just on end points
The electrostatic force is conservative: its work is path-independent
Answer: Because the electrostatic force is conservative
quiz.mistake: Links potential energy to the strength of the force

quiz.q: A charge is moved from A to B along three different paths. The work done by the electrostatic force is
quiz.explain: For a conservative force the work depends only on the end points.
steps: Work by a conservative force depends only on start and end points
All three paths join A and B, so the work is equal
Answer: the same for all paths
quiz.mistake: Thinks work depends on path length

quiz.q: Why do we bring the test charge 'slowly' when defining potential?
options: So that the charge does not lose mass
So that the field becomes uniform
So that the charge is not quantised
So that no kinetic energy is gained and all work goes into potential energy
quiz.explain: Moving it without acceleration means the external force just balances the electric force.
steps: Moving slowly means no acceleration and no gain of kinetic energy
Then the external force just balances the field and all work becomes U
Answer: So that no kinetic energy is gained and all work goes into potential energy

quiz.q: The potential difference between two points is 12 V. How much work is done by an external agent in moving 3 C slowly from the lower to the higher potential (in J)?
Which of these is physically meaningful in electrostatics?
options: The absolute potential at a point without a reference
The potential energy of a single charge without a reference
The value of potential at infinity
The potential difference between two points
quiz.explain: Adding a constant to all potentials changes nothing physical; only differences matter.
steps: Adding a constant to all potentials changes nothing physical
So only potential differences can be measured
Answer: The potential difference between two points
quiz.mistake: Thinks potential has an absolute value

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The work done by an electrostatic field in moving a charge around a closed loop is zero. Reason (R): The electrostatic force is conservative. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: For a conservative force, returning to the start means no net work.
steps: A: work by the field round a closed loop is zero – true
R: electrostatic force is conservative – true

quiz.q: A charge of -2 µC is brought slowly from infinity to a point where V = 500 V. What work is done by the external agent (in mJ)?

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Is the potential at my nest absolutely 100 V, or 100 V compared with something?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Potential is work per unit charge, measured from a chosen zero such as infinity. Only differences matter!
teach.nudge: Good! What does potential measure, and what is it measured relative to?

revise.summary: The electrostatic force is conservative, so electric potential energy can be defined; only its differences matter. Electric potential V is the work per unit positive charge to bring a test charge slowly from infinity: V = W/q.

remember: Zero of potential is a choice; usually at infinity
traps: Don't drop the sign of q when finding work
Absolute potential has no meaning without a reference

topics.title: Potential due to a point charge

learn.hook: A nucleus creates a potential 'hill'. Climbing it with a positive charge costs energy, and the hill gets taller as 1/r the closer you get.
points: Potential difference V_B - V_A = work per unit positive charge from A to B. Unit: volt, 1 V = 1 J C⁻¹.
Integrating E = kQ/r² from infinity to r gives V(r) = Q/(4πε₀r) = kQ/r.
V is positive for positive Q and negative for negative Q, and it falls off as 1/r (slower than E ∝ 1/r²).
Work to bring q from infinity to a point at potential V: W = qV.
For two opposite charges, V = 0 at points where kq₁/r₁ + kq₂/r₂ = 0, which lies between them and also outside, beyond the smaller charge.

learn.reallife: The 'Danger 11000 V' boards on Indian power poles are about potential: a large potential difference means each coulomb of charge carries a lot of energy through anything that bridges it.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'The field drops as 1/r², does the potential drop the same way?'
teach.praise: Chirp! V = kQ/r goes as 1/r, slower than the field's 1/r². Super clear!
teach.nudge: Nearly! Write the formula for V of a point charge. What power of r is in it?

revise.summary: A point charge Q gives potential V = kQ/r, positive for positive and negative for negative Q, falling as 1/r. Work to bring q from infinity is W = qV, and for opposite charges V = 0 at one point between them and one beyond the smaller charge.
traps: V ∝ 1/r, not 1/r²
For opposite charges the outside zero is not beyond the larger charge; it lies beyond the smaller one

learn.hook: Potential is a scalar. No arrows, no components: just add numbers with signs. That makes it the friendliest tool in electrostatics.
points: Superposition: V at a point due to many charges = algebraic sum k(q₁/r₁ + q₂/r₂ + ...).
Dipole potential (r ≫ a): V = p cosθ/(4πε₀r²), where θ is the angle between p and the position vector.
On the axis (θ = 0 or 180°) V = ±kp/r², the largest magnitude; on the equatorial plane (θ = 90°) V = 0.
Dipole potential depends on direction (θ) as well as distance, and falls as 1/r², faster than a point charge's 1/r.
For charges at the corners of a regular polygon, every charge is the same distance from the centre, so V(centre) = k(Σq)/r.

example.q: Charges of +2 µC, +2 µC, -1 µC and +1 µC sit at the corners of a square, each 0.3 m from the centre. Find V at the centre.

learn.reallife: Doctors reading an ECG at AIIMS are looking at potential differences produced by the heart, which behaves roughly like a rotating electric dipole as it beats.

quiz.mistake: Ignores the sign of the -5 nC charge

quiz.q: Why is it often easier to find the potential than the field due to several charges?
options: Potential does not depend on distance
Potential is a scalar, so contributions add algebraically
quiz.explain: No directions or components are needed for a scalar sum.
steps: Field is a vector: needs directions and components
Potential is a scalar: contributions just add with signs

quiz.q: Assertion (A): At points on the equatorial plane of a dipole, the potential is zero but the field is not. Reason (R): Potential is a scalar sum, while the field is a vector sum. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Equal and opposite potentials cancel as numbers; the fields' components along the axis add instead of cancelling.
steps: A: on the equatorial plane V = 0 but E ≠ 0 – true
R: V is a scalar sum, E a vector sum – true
+kq/r and −kq/r cancel as numbers, but the fields' components add; R explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Assumes zero potential means zero field

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'On the dipole's middle line, potential is zero. So there's no field there either?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Zero potential, but the vector fields add up along -p. Potential and field are different things!
teach.nudge: Good! Is potential a vector or a scalar? What about the field?

revise.summary: Potentials of several charges add as scalars. A short dipole has V = kp cosθ/r²: ±kp/r² on the axis and zero on the equatorial plane, falling as 1/r². For a regular polygon, V(centre) = kΣq/r.
focus: Dipole potential and its angular dependence
Potential at the centre of symmetric arrangements
traps: Add potentials with signs, not as vectors
Dipole potential ∝ 1/r², not 1/r³

learn.hook: Contour lines on a hill map join points of equal height. Bunched-up contours mean a steep slope. Equipotential surfaces do the same for electric fields.
points: An equipotential surface has the same potential at every point, so no work is done in moving a charge along it.
The electric field is always normal to equipotential surfaces (otherwise a component along the surface would do work).
Shapes: concentric spheres for a point charge, parallel planes perpendicular to a uniform field; distorted shapes for a dipole and for two like charges.
E = -dV/dl: the field points in the direction of steepest decrease of potential, with magnitude |ΔV|/Δl measured normal to the equipotentials.
Closely spaced equipotentials mean a strong field; widely spaced ones mean a weak field.

example.q: Two equipotential planes 5 cm apart differ by 10 V. Find E.
steps: = 200 V m⁻¹, from the higher to the lower potential

learn.reallife: Survey of India's topographic maps show height contours; electrical engineers draw equipotential maps around substations to keep 'step voltage' safe for people walking nearby.

games.title: Equipotential truths

ΔV = 0, so W = qΔV = 0.
The electric field can be parallel to an equipotential surface.
E is always perpendicular to it.
E points in the direction in which potential increases fastest.
E points towards decreasing potential.
Two different equipotential surfaces can intersect.
That point would have two potentials.
The unit V m⁻¹ is the same as N C⁻¹.
Both are units of electric field.

quiz.q: Equipotentials are 2 cm apart and differ by 4 V each in a uniform field. What is the field strength (in V m⁻¹)?

quiz.explain: ΔV = 0 along an equipotential, so W = 0.

quiz.q: The equipotential surfaces of an isolated point charge are

quiz.explain: V = kQ/r is constant where r is constant.

Points at fixed r form spheres centred on the charge
Answer: concentric spheres centred on the charge

quiz.q: In a region, V changes from 30 V to 10 V over 4 mm along x. What is the field along x (in V m⁻¹)?
quiz.explain: Ex = -dV/dx = -(10 - 30)/0.004 = +5000 V m⁻¹. The field points towards lower potential (+x).
quiz.mistake: Drops the minus sign of E = -dV/dx

quiz.q: Why must the electric field be perpendicular to an equipotential surface?
options: If E had a component along the surface, moving a charge along it would need work, contradicting constant V
Because the surface is a conductor
quiz.explain: Zero work along the surface means zero field component along it.
steps: Moving along an equipotential needs no work
A field component along the surface would do work
So E has no component along the surface: it is normal to it
Answer: If E had a component along the surface, moving a charge along it would need work, contradicting constant V
quiz.mistake: Gives a reason based on shape instead of work

quiz.q: In the region where equipotentials are drawn closer together, the field is
quiz.explain: E = ΔV/Δl; smaller Δl for the same ΔV gives larger E.
steps: Same ΔV over a smaller Δl gives a larger E

quiz.q: For a uniform field along +x, the equipotential surfaces are
options: planes parallel to the y-z plane
planes parallel to the x-y plane
quiz.explain: They must be perpendicular to E, i.e., perpendicular to x.
steps: E along +x ⇒ surfaces perpendicular to x, i.e. parallel to the y-z plane
Answer: planes parallel to the y-z plane
quiz.mistake: Places planes parallel to the field

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Two equipotential surfaces never intersect. Reason (R): At an intersection point, the potential would have two different values. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Potential at a point has a single value, so two different equipotentials cannot share a point.
steps: A: equipotential surfaces never intersect – true
R: at an intersection V would have two values – true
V has a single value at a point, so R explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Does not connect the reason to the assertion

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Which way does the electric field point compared to equipotential surfaces?'
teach.praise: Chirp! E is normal to equipotentials, pointing from high to low potential. And no work along them!
teach.nudge: Close! Think about the work done along an equipotential. What does that say about E's direction?

revise.summary: An equipotential surface has the same potential everywhere, so no work is done along it and E is normal to it. E = −dV/dl points towards decreasing potential, and closely spaced equipotentials mean a strong field.
remember: Point charge: spheres; uniform field: parallel planes
traps: E does not point towards higher potential; it points from higher to lower
Don't calculate non-zero work along an equipotential; it is zero

topics.title: Potential energy of a system of charges

learn.hook: To pack charges into a tiny space you must fight their repulsion. That fight stores energy, like compressing a spring, and nuclear fission later releases it.
points: Two charges: U = q₁q₂/(4πε₀r₁₂) = kq₁q₂/r₁₂, the work needed to assemble them from infinity.
Like charges: U > 0 (work must be done to push them together). Unlike charges: U < 0 (they attract, so work is released).
Three or more charges: add U for every pair, U = k(q₁q₂/r₁₂ + q₁q₃/r₁₃ + q₂q₃/r₂₃).
Work by an external agent to change a configuration = U(final) - U(initial).
Four charges at the corners of a square have six pairs: four sides and two diagonals.

example.q: Find the work needed to place three charges of 1 µC each at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side 0.1 m.

learn.reallife: Inside a uranium nucleus in a reactor at Kudankulam or Tarapur, protons are packed so tightly that their Coulomb potential energy is enormous. When the nucleus splits, part of that energy is released.

quiz.mistake: Ignores the signs of the charges

quiz.q: Four charges of +1 µC each are at the corners of a square of side 0.3 m. How many pairs must be counted in the total potential energy?

quiz.q: Three charges of 2 µC each are placed at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side 0.3 m. What is the total potential energy (in J)? (k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
quiz.explain: Each pair: 9 × 10⁹ × 4 × 10⁻¹²/0.3 = 0.12 J. Three pairs: 0.36 J.

teach.ask: Gappu wants to know: 'How do I find the energy stored in a gang of four charges?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Add kq₁q₂/r for every pair: four charges means six pairs. Awesome!
teach.nudge: Good start! What do we calculate for each pair of charges, and then what do we do?

revise.summary: The potential energy of two charges is U = kq₁q₂/r, the work to assemble them from infinity; it is positive for like and negative for unlike charges. For many charges add U for every pair; external work = U(final) − U(initial).
focus: U for a pair and its sign
traps: Don't drop the sign of each charge
Don't forget diagonal pairs in a square

topics.title: Potential energy in an external field and the electron volt

learn.hook: An electron accelerated through a single volt gains a tiny 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Physicists liked that unit so much they gave it a name: the electron volt.
points: A charge q at a point where an external potential is V(r) has potential energy qV(r). The external field's sources are taken as fixed.
Electron volt: energy gained by an electron (or lost) when it moves through a potential difference of 1 V. 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Also keV, MeV.
A charge q accelerated through ΔV gains kinetic energy qΔV.
Two charges q₁, q₂ in an external field: U = q₁V(r₁) + q₂V(r₂) + kq₁q₂/r₁₂. The last term is their mutual energy.
An electron (negative) gains energy moving towards higher potential; a proton gains energy moving towards lower potential.

example.q: A proton is accelerated from rest through 1000 V. Find its kinetic energy in eV and J.

learn.reallife: Old CRT televisions, still found in some Indian homes, accelerated electrons through about 20 kV, giving each one roughly 20 keV of energy before it hit the screen to make it glow.

quiz.explain: K = eΔV = 500 eV.

quiz.q: Two charges 5 µC and -3 µC are placed 15 cm apart, both on the V = 0 equipotential of an external field. What is the system's potential energy (in J)? (k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)

teach.ask: Gappu sees '13.6 eV' in a book. 'Is an electron volt a kind of volt?'
teach.praise: Chirp! An eV is energy: what an electron gains across 1 volt, 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Got it!
teach.nudge: Good! Is the eV a unit of potential or of energy? How is it defined?

revise.summary: A charge q at external potential V has energy qV; accelerating through ΔV gives kinetic energy qΔV. 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; for two charges in an external field, add their mutual energy kq₁q₂/r₁₂.

System of two charges in an external field
traps: eV is a unit of energy, not potential

topics.title: Potential energy of a dipole in a field

learn.hook: A compass needle settles pointing north and wobbles back if nudged. A dipole in an electric field has the same favourite direction, set by its potential energy.
points: Potential energy of a dipole in a uniform field: U(θ) = -pE cosθ = -p·E (taking U = 0 at θ = 90°).
θ = 0 (p along E): U = -pE, minimum, stable equilibrium.
θ = 180° (p opposite E): U = +pE, maximum, unstable equilibrium.
Work done by an external agent to rotate a dipole from θ₁ to θ₂: W = pE(cosθ₁ - cosθ₂).
Turning a dipole from stable (0°) to unstable (180°) needs W = 2pE.

example.q: A dipole p = 2 × 10⁻²⁹ C m is in a field of 10⁶ N C⁻¹. Find the work to turn it from 0° to 90°.

learn.reallife: Liquid crystal displays in phones assembled in Noida rely on molecular dipoles: applying a field rotates them to their minimum-energy orientation, switching pixels on and off.

games.title: Stable or not?
items: A dipole aligned along the field is in stable equilibrium.
U is minimum at θ = 0.
A dipole antiparallel to the field feels a large torque.
At 180° the torque pE sinθ is zero, though equilibrium is unstable.
U = -pE cosθ.
That is the standard expression.
Work to rotate a dipole from 90° to 0° is positive.
U falls from 0 to -pE, so the external work is -pE (the field does the work).
The potential energy of a dipole is maximum at θ = 180°.
U = +pE there.

quiz.q: A dipole p = 5 × 10⁻⁹ C m is at θ = 0° in a field of 2 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹. What is its potential energy (in units of 10⁻⁴ J)?

In which orientation is an electric dipole in unstable equilibrium in a uniform field?
quiz.explain: At 180° torque is zero but U is maximum, so any tilt makes it rotate away.
steps: Torque is zero there, but any tilt rotates it away

quiz.q: A molecule with p = 10⁻²⁹ C m is turned from θ = 0° to θ = 60° in a field of 10⁶ N C⁻¹. What work is needed (in units of 10⁻²⁴ J)?
quiz.mistake: Uses sin 60° in place of cos 60°

quiz.q: The expression U = -p·E for a dipole assumes U = 0 when
quiz.explain: -pE cos 90° = 0, so the reference is θ = 90°.
steps: Answer: p is perpendicular to E
quiz.mistake: Thinks the reference is at θ = 0

quiz.q: At which angle are both the torque and the potential energy of the dipole zero?
options: No angle: U = 0 at 90°, where the torque is maximum
quiz.explain: U = 0 at 90°, where τ = pE is maximum; τ = 0 at 0° and 180°, where U = ∓pE ≠ 0.
steps: U = 0 only at 90°, where τ = pE sin90° is maximum
τ = 0 only at 0° and 180°, where U = ∓pE ≠ 0
So they are never both zero
Answer: No angle: U = 0 at 90°, where the torque is maximum
quiz.mistake: Assumes torque and energy vanish together

quiz.q: A dipole in a field of 10⁴ N C⁻¹ has a potential energy of -3 × 10⁻⁵ J when aligned with the field. What is p (in nC m)?
quiz.explain: U = -pE, so p = 3 × 10⁻⁵/10⁴ = 3 × 10⁻⁹ C m = 3 nC m.
quiz.mistake: Keeps the negative sign in p

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A dipole placed in a uniform field tends to align with the field. Reason (R): Its potential energy is minimum when p is along E. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Systems move towards minimum potential energy; the torque rotates p into line with E.
steps: A: a dipole tends to align with the field – true
R: U is minimum when p is along E – true
Systems move to minimum U, so R explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Does not relate the torque to the energy minimum

teach.ask: Gappu tilted a dipole in a field: 'Why does it swing back to point along the field?'
teach.praise: Chirp! U = -pE cosθ is lowest at θ = 0, and the torque turns it back there. Stable!
teach.nudge: Nice! Where is the dipole's potential energy lowest, and what pushes it there?

revise.summary: A dipole in a uniform field has U = −pE cosθ, minimum (stable) when p is along E and maximum (unstable) when opposite. Work to rotate it from θ₁ to θ₂ is pE(cosθ₁ − cosθ₂).
traps: U = 0 at 90°, not at 0°
Use cosθ₁ − cosθ₂, not the reverse

learn.hook: Copper is full of free electrons. Put it in a field and they rush around until they have cancelled the field inside. That simple fact gives conductors five superpowers.
points: Inside a conductor (in electrostatic equilibrium) the field is zero; free charges rearrange until the internal field vanishes.
Just outside, the field is normal to the surface; a tangential part would push charges along the surface.
There is no net charge in the interior; any excess charge sits on the outer surface.
The whole conductor (inside and surface) is at one potential: it is an equipotential volume.
Just outside, E = (σ/ε₀) n̂, with σ the local surface charge density and n̂ the outward normal.

example.q: A conducting surface has σ = 2.6 × 10⁻⁶ C m⁻². Find the field just outside. (ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²)
steps: ≈ 2.9 × 10⁵ N C⁻¹, normal to the surface
example.answer: ≈ 2.9 × 10⁵ N C⁻¹, outward along the normal

learn.reallife: Metal cabinets of ATMs and server racks in Bengaluru data centres stay at one potential and are earthed, so stray charge never builds up across the electronics inside.

games.title: Conductor rules
items: In electrostatics, the field inside a conductor is zero.
Free charges cancel any internal field.
Excess charge on a conductor spreads evenly through its volume.
It lives on the outer surface.
Just outside a charged conductor, the field is normal to the surface.
A tangential component would move charges.
Different points on the surface of a charged conductor can be at different potentials.
The conductor is an equipotential.
The field just outside a conductor is σ/(2ε₀).
For a conductor it is σ/ε₀; σ/(2ε₀) is for a thin sheet.

games.title: How a conductor reaches equilibrium
games.prompt: Put the events in order when a conductor is placed in a field
items: External field acts on free electrons
Electrons drift opposite to the field
Charge piles up on the surfaces
Induced charges create an opposing field
Net field inside becomes zero and charges stop

quiz.q: What is the electric field inside a solid metal sphere carrying 5 µC, in electrostatic equilibrium (in N C⁻¹)?
quiz.explain: In equilibrium the field inside any conductor is zero.
steps: In electrostatic equilibrium free charges rearrange until the inside field vanishes

quiz.q: Where does excess charge given to an isolated conductor reside?
options: Only at its sharpest point and nowhere else
quiz.explain: Gauss's law with E = 0 inside shows no charge in the interior.
steps: E = 0 inside, so a Gaussian surface just inside encloses no charge
Excess charge must sit on the outer surface

quiz.q: A charged conductor has potential 200 V at its surface. What is the potential at its centre (in V)?
quiz.explain: E = 0 inside, so V does not change from surface to centre.
steps: So V does not change from the surface to the centre
quiz.mistake: Thinks zero field means zero potential

quiz.q: A conductor has σ = 8.85 × 10⁻⁸ C m⁻². What is the field just outside (in kN C⁻¹)? (ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²)
Why is the electrostatic field at the surface of a conductor normal to it?
options: Any tangential component would move surface charges, so equilibrium needs it to vanish
Because the field inside is non-zero
quiz.explain: In equilibrium charges are at rest, so no force along the surface.
steps: In equilibrium surface charges are at rest
A tangential field would push them along the surface
So only the normal component remains
Answer: Any tangential component would move surface charges, so equilibrium needs it to vanish
quiz.mistake: Gives a geometric rather than a physical reason

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A conductor in electrostatic equilibrium is an equipotential. Reason (R): The field inside and the tangential field on its surface are zero. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: With no field along any path within or on the conductor, no work is done, so V is the same everywhere.
steps: A: a conductor in equilibrium is an equipotential – true
R: field inside and tangential field on surface are zero – true
No field along any path ⇒ no work ⇒ same V; R explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Misses the link between zero field and constant potential

quiz.q: The surface charge density at a point on a conductor is doubled. The field just outside that point
quiz.explain: E = σ/ε₀ is proportional to σ.

quiz.q: A neutral metal slab is placed in a uniform external field. Which statement is correct?
options: Negative charge appears on the face where the field enters and positive on the face where it leaves
Positive charge appears where the field enters
quiz.explain: Electrons drift against the field to the entry face; the other face is left positive. Their field cancels the external field inside.
steps: Free electrons drift opposite to E, towards the face where the field enters
That face becomes negative; the exit face is left positive
Their field cancels the external field inside
Answer: Negative charge appears on the face where the field enters and positive on the face where it leaves

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why is there no electric field inside a metal spoon kept near a charged comb?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Free electrons shift to the surface until their field cancels the outside field inside the metal. Smart!
teach.nudge: Good! What do the free electrons in the metal do when a field acts on them?

revise.summary: In electrostatic equilibrium the field inside a conductor is zero, excess charge lies on its outer surface, the field just outside is normal with E = σ/ε₀, and the whole conductor is an equipotential.
focus: Induced charges in an external field
remember: E = 0 inside; no charge in the interior
Field at surface is normal; E = σ/ε₀
traps: V inside is not zero; it equals the surface potential
Electrons do not gather where the field leaves; they gather on the face where it enters

topics.title: Shielding, sharp points and charged shells

learn.hook: During a thunderstorm on the Mumbai-Pune expressway, the safest place is inside your car. The metal body acts as an electrostatic shield.
points: Electrostatic shielding: the field inside any empty cavity of a conductor is zero, whatever the outside fields or charges. Sensitive instruments are kept in metal enclosures.

Charge on a conductor concentrates where the surface is most curved (sharp points), giving large σ and large fields; air can break down there (corona discharge). Lightning conductors use sharp points.
Charge q placed inside a cavity of a neutral conducting shell induces -q on the cavity wall and +q on the outer surface.
Uniformly charged shell of radius R: V = kq/r outside (r ≥ R) and V = kq/R, constant, everywhere inside.
Inside the shell E = 0 but V is not zero; it equals the surface potential.

example.q: A shell of radius 0.1 m carries 2 nC. Find V at its centre and at 0.3 m from the centre.
example.answer: 180 V at the centre; 60 V at 0.3 m

learn.reallife: Tall buildings in Kolkata and temple towers often carry a pointed copper lightning conductor connected to an earthed plate. The point helps discharge build-up, and the conductor guides strikes safely to the ground.

games.title: Shielding facts
items: The field inside a cavity in a conductor is zero even when there are charges outside the conductor.
That is electrostatic shielding.
Charge density is greatest at the flattest part of a conductor.
It is greatest at sharp, highly curved parts.
The potential inside a charged hollow shell is zero.
It is constant and equal to kq/R.
A charge q inside a cavity induces -q on the cavity wall.
So that the field inside the conductor's material is zero.
Sitting inside a car during lightning is safer than standing in an open field.
The metal body shields the inside.

quiz.q: A thin shell of radius 0.2 m carries 4 nC. What is the potential at a point 0.1 m from its centre (in V)? (k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
quiz.explain: Inside the shell V is constant and equal to kq/R = 36/0.2 = 180 V.
steps: Inside a shell V is constant = kq/R
quiz.mistake: Uses the distance from the centre instead of R, or takes V = 0 inside

quiz.q: For the same shell (4 nC, R = 0.2 m), what is the potential at 0.4 m from the centre (in V)?
quiz.explain: Outside V = kq/r = 36/0.4 = 90 V.

quiz.q: Why does a lightning conductor have pointed tips?
options: Charge density and field are very high at sharp points, so charge leaks away into the air
quiz.explain: High σ at points gives strong fields that ionise air, enabling discharge.
steps: Charge crowds at sharp points, so σ and E = σ/ε₀ are very large there
The strong field ionises air and charge leaks away safely
Answer: Charge density and field are very high at sharp points, so charge leaks away into the air

quiz.q: A charge +q is placed at the centre of a cavity in a neutral conducting sphere. What charges appear on the inner and outer surfaces?
options: -q on the inner surface, +q on the outer surface
quiz.explain: The inner wall gets -q so that E = 0 in the metal; the outer surface gets +q since the conductor is neutral overall.
steps: E = 0 in the metal ⇒ inner wall must carry −q
The shell is neutral, so the outer surface gets +q
Answer: -q on the inner surface, +q on the outer surface
quiz.mistake: Forgets that the conductor stays neutral overall

quiz.q: Which is the best example of electrostatic shielding?
options: Keeping a sensitive instrument inside a closed metal box
Using a long copper wire as an antenna
quiz.explain: The field inside a closed conducting enclosure is zero.
steps: The field inside a closed conducting enclosure is zero
So a metal box shields an instrument from outside fields
Answer: Keeping a sensitive instrument inside a closed metal box

quiz.q: A conducting sphere of radius 9 cm has a potential of 200 V at its surface. What is the charge on it (in nC)? (k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
quiz.mistake: Uses R in cm without converting

quiz.q: A hollow conducting sphere carries charge Q₁. A small charge Q₂ is placed at its centre. The field outside the sphere at distance r from the centre is
quiz.explain: The outer surface ends up with Q₁ + Q₂ (the original Q₁ plus the induced +Q₂), so Gauss's law gives k(Q₁ + Q₂)/r².
steps: Q₂ at the centre induces −Q₂ on the inner surface and +Q₂ on the outer
Gauss's law outside: E = k(Q₁ + Q₂)/r²
quiz.mistake: Ignores the induced charge on the outer surface

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Corona discharge is seen near sharp points of high-voltage conductors. Reason (R): Surface charge density is larger at points of smaller radius of curvature. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
quiz.explain: Large σ means large field σ/ε₀, which ionises the surrounding air.
steps: A: corona discharge occurs near sharp points – true
R: σ is larger where radius of curvature is smaller – true
Large σ ⇒ large field σ/ε₀ ⇒ air ionises; R explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Does not link curvature with charge density

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If lightning hits a car, why are people inside safe?'
teach.praise: Chirp! The metal body is a conducting shell: charge stays on the outside and the field inside is zero. Safe!
teach.nudge: Good! What is special about the field inside a closed conductor?

revise.summary: The field inside a conductor's cavity is zero (electrostatic shielding). Charge concentrates at sharp points, causing corona discharge; a charge in a cavity induces −q inside and +q outside; a shell has V = kq/R inside and kq/r outside.
focus: Charge at sharp points and lightning conductors
Charges induced by a charge in a cavity; shell potential
remember: Shell: V = kq/R inside (constant), kq/r outside
Charge q in cavity → −q on inner wall, +q on outer surface
traps: Inside a shell V is not zero, though E = 0
Sharp points have higher, not lower, σ

learn.hook: Put a slab of glass between charged plates and the field inside weakens. The glass has no free electrons, yet it fights back. How?
points: Dielectrics are insulators. Unlike conductors, they have no free charges, but their molecules get polarised in a field, which only partly reduces the field inside.
Polar molecules (e.g. H₂O) have permanent dipoles that align with the field; non-polar molecules get induced dipoles by charge separation.
Polarisation P = dipole moment per unit volume. For linear dielectrics P = χe E, where χe is the electric susceptibility.
A uniformly polarised slab acquires bound surface charges ±σp on its faces. These produce a field opposite to the applied one, so the field inside is reduced (not cancelled).
Contrast: inside a conductor E becomes exactly zero; inside a dielectric E is only reduced.

example.q: A slab is placed in a uniform field E₀. Its bound charges produce an opposing field of E₀/4. Find the net field inside.
steps: The dielectric reduces but does not cancel the field

learn.reallife: Mica and ceramic are used as insulating dielectrics in capacitors on the circuit boards of Indian-made smartphones and EV chargers.

games.title: Polar or non-polar dielectric molecule
items: H₂O
HCl
CO₂
O₂
N₂
NH₃

games.title: Dielectric facts
items: A dielectric placed in a field has zero field inside, like a conductor.
The field is reduced, not cancelled.
Polarisation is the dipole moment per unit volume.
That is its definition.
Non-polar molecules can become dipoles in an external field.
These are induced dipoles.
Bound surface charges on a polarised slab can flow away if touched by a wire.
Bound charges are tied to molecules; they are not free.
The field due to bound charges inside the slab opposes the applied field.
That is why the net field is reduced.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between a conductor and a dielectric placed in an electric field?
options: Both make the field zero inside
A dielectric increases the field inside
The field inside a conductor becomes zero, but inside a dielectric it is only reduced
A conductor only reduces the field
quiz.explain: Free charges in a conductor cancel the field; bound charges in a dielectric only partly oppose it.
steps: Conductor: free charges cancel the field, so E inside = 0
Dielectric: bound charges only partly oppose it
Answer: The field inside a conductor becomes zero, but inside a dielectric it is only reduced
quiz.mistake: Treats a dielectric like a conductor

quiz.q: Polarisation P of a dielectric is defined as
quiz.explain: P = total dipole moment / volume.
steps: Polarisation P = total dipole moment ÷ volume
Answer: dipole moment per unit volume
quiz.mistake: Confuses polarisation with surface charge density

quiz.q: In the relation P = χe E, the quantity χe is called the
quiz.explain: χe measures how strongly a material polarises in response to the field.
steps: P = χe E for a linear dielectric

quiz.q: A non-polar molecule placed in an electric field
options: develops an induced dipole moment along the field
gets a permanent dipole moment opposite to the field
quiz.explain: The field pushes the nucleus and electron cloud apart, inducing a dipole along E.
steps: The field pushes the nucleus and electron cloud apart
This creates an induced dipole along E
Answer: develops an induced dipole moment along the field
quiz.mistake: Thinks the molecule gains net charge

quiz.q: Why do polar molecules not show any net polarisation without an external field?
options: Their dipoles always cancel inside each molecule
Their permanent dipoles point in random directions due to thermal motion
They are all aligned opposite to each other in pairs
quiz.explain: Random orientations average out; an applied field partly aligns them.
steps: Each polar molecule has a permanent dipole
Thermal motion points them in random directions, so they average to zero
Answer: Their permanent dipoles point in random directions due to thermal motion

quiz.q: A dielectric slab in an applied field E₀ has a net internal field of 0.2E₀. What field do its bound charges produce (in terms of E₀, opposing)?
quiz.explain: Net = E₀ - E_bound, so E_bound = E₀ - 0.2E₀ = 0.8E₀.
quiz.mistake: Gives the net field instead of the bound-charge field

quiz.q: Where do the bound charges of a uniformly polarised dielectric slab appear?
options: On its two faces perpendicular to the field
On the faces parallel to the field
quiz.explain: Inside, neighbouring dipole charges cancel; only the end faces have uncancelled bound charge.
steps: Only the two faces perpendicular to the field keep uncancelled bound charge
Answer: On its two faces perpendicular to the field
quiz.mistake: Puts the bound charge in the volume

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A dielectric reduces the field between capacitor plates. Reason (R): Bound charges on its surfaces produce a field opposing the applied field. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: The opposing field of the induced surface charges reduces the net field.
steps: A: a dielectric reduces the field between plates – true
R: bound surface charges produce an opposing field – true
That opposing field is the cause, so R explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Does not see how bound charges create an opposing field

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Glass has no free electrons. How can it weaken an electric field?'
teach.praise: Chirp! The molecules become dipoles, bound surface charges appear, and their field opposes the applied one. Wow!
teach.nudge: Good! What happens to the molecules of glass in a field, and what charges appear on its surfaces?

revise.summary: Dielectrics have no free charges but polarise in a field: polar molecules align and non-polar ones get induced dipoles. Polarisation P = χeE creates bound surface charges whose opposing field reduces, but does not cancel, the field inside.
remember: P = dipole moment per unit volume = χeE
Bound charges appear on faces perpendicular to E
Net field = applied − bound field (reduced, not zero)
traps: A dielectric does not make the field zero
Polar molecules show no net P without a field

learn.hook: A camera flash charges up in a second and fires its energy in a millisecond. The little device that holds that charge is a capacitor.
points: A capacitor is two conductors separated by an insulator, carrying charges +Q and -Q.
Capacitance C = Q/V, where V is the potential difference between the plates. Unit: farad (1 F = 1 C V⁻¹). Practical units: µF (10⁻⁶ F), nF (10⁻⁹ F), pF (10⁻¹² F).
C depends only on the geometry (size, shape, separation) and the medium between the conductors, not on Q or V.
Too high a voltage makes the field exceed the dielectric strength (about 3 × 10⁶ V m⁻¹ for air), and the medium breaks down. Circuit symbol: two parallel lines.
Parallel plate capacitor: field between the plates is σ/ε₀ (σ = Q/A) and practically zero outside, ignoring fringing at the edges.

example.q: A capacitor stores 60 µC when connected to a 12 V supply. Find C. What charge does it hold at 24 V?
steps: C does not change with V
example.answer: C = 5 µF; Q = 120 µC at 24 V

learn.reallife: The ceiling fans in most Indian homes use a 2–4 µF capacitor to help the motor start; when a fan hums but will not spin, a technician often replaces this capacitor.

games.title: Capacitance check
items: Doubling the charge on a capacitor doubles its capacitance.
C = Q/V; V also doubles, so C is unchanged.
Capacitance depends on the medium between the plates.
A dielectric increases C.
Between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor, E = σ/ε₀.
The two sheet fields add.
Outside an ideal parallel plate capacitor, E = σ/ε₀.
Outside, the fields cancel to zero.
If the voltage across a capacitor is too high, the dielectric can break down.
The field exceeds the dielectric strength.

quiz.q: A capacitor holds 40 µC at 8 V. What is its capacitance (in µF)?
A 10 µF capacitor is connected to a 9 V battery. What charge does it store (in µC)?
quiz.explain: Q = CV = 10 µF × 9 V = 90 µC.

quiz.q: The potential difference across a capacitor is doubled. Its capacitance
quiz.explain: C depends on geometry and medium only; Q doubles instead.
steps: C depends only on geometry and medium
Doubling V doubles Q; C = Q/V is unchanged

quiz.q: A parallel plate capacitor's plates have σ = 17.7 × 10⁻⁹ C m⁻². What is the field between them (in V m⁻¹)? (ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²)
Why is there a maximum safe voltage rating printed on a capacitor?
options: Above it, the plates melt from current flow
Above it, the field in the dielectric exceeds its dielectric strength and the dielectric breaks down
quiz.explain: Breakdown ionises the insulator and lets charge leak across.
steps: Field in the dielectric E = V/d rises with voltage
Above the rating E exceeds the dielectric strength and the dielectric breaks down
Answer: Above it, the field in the dielectric exceeds its dielectric strength and the dielectric breaks down

quiz.q: Air breaks down at about 3 × 10⁶ V m⁻¹. What is the largest voltage that can be applied across an air gap of 1 mm (in kV)?
quiz.mistake: Slips a power of ten in the mm conversion

quiz.q: The field outside an ideal parallel plate capacitor (away from the edges) is
quiz.explain: Fields of the +σ and -σ plates cancel outside.
steps: Outside the plates the +σ and −σ fields are equal and opposite
quiz.mistake: Thinks each plate's field leaks out

quiz.q: A capacitor consists of
options: two insulators separated by a conductor
two conductors separated by an insulator
a coil of wire around an iron core
quiz.explain: The insulator keeps the charges ±Q apart on the two conductors.
steps: A capacitor holds +Q and −Q on two conductors
An insulator between them keeps the charges apart
Answer: two conductors separated by an insulator
quiz.mistake: Confuses a capacitor with an inductor

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If I put more charge on a capacitor, does its capacitance increase?'
teach.praise: Chirp! C = Q/V stays the same; it is set by the geometry and the medium. More charge just means more voltage!
teach.nudge: Close! What does capacitance depend on? Does V change when Q changes?

revise.summary: A capacitor is two conductors separated by an insulator holding ±Q. C = Q/V depends only on geometry and medium; units are farads (µF, nF, pF), and too high a voltage breaks down the dielectric.
focus: Dielectric strength and field of a parallel plate capacitor
traps: Changing V changes Q, not C
Don't substitute µF or mm directly; convert to SI units

topics.title: Parallel plate capacitor with and without dielectric

learn.hook: How big would a 1 farad parallel plate capacitor with a 1 cm air gap be? Larger than many Indian cities! The farad is a giant unit.
points: Derivation: E = σ/ε₀ = Q/(ε₀A), V = Ed = Qd/(ε₀A), so C = Q/V = ε₀A/d.
With C = 1 F and d = 1 cm, A = Cd/ε₀ ≈ 1.1 × 10⁹ m², a square about 33 km on each side. Real capacitors are in µF to pF.
With a dielectric filling the gap (charge fixed), the field becomes E₀/K and V becomes V₀/K.
So C = Kε₀A/d = KC₀. Dielectric constant K = ε/ε₀ (relative permittivity) is greater than 1; ε = Kε₀ is the permittivity of the medium. In terms of susceptibility, K = 1 + χe/ε₀.
Typical K values: vacuum 1, air about 1.0006, water about 80, mica about 6, glass 5 to 10.

example.q: A parallel plate capacitor has A = 0.02 m² and d = 1.77 mm, in air. Find C, and C when mica (K = 6) fills the gap. (ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²)
example.answer: 100 pF in air; 600 pF with mica

learn.reallife: Touchscreens on phones sold across India work as tiny capacitors: your finger, which is mostly water with high permittivity, changes the local capacitance and the phone senses where you touched.

items.text: Doubling plate area makes C ___.
Doubling the plate separation makes C ___.
Filling with a dielectric of K = 4 makes C ___ times larger.
With charge fixed, a dielectric makes V ___ by K.

quiz.q: A parallel plate capacitor has plates of area 0.1 m² separated by 0.885 mm in air. What is its capacitance (in nF)? (ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²)
quiz.mistake: Forgets to convert mm to m

quiz.q: The gap of a 20 pF air capacitor is completely filled with a dielectric of K = 5. What is the new capacitance (in pF)?
quiz.mistake: Divides by K instead of multiplying

quiz.q: The plate separation of a parallel plate capacitor is tripled and its plate area is doubled. The capacitance becomes
A charged capacitor is disconnected from the battery and a dielectric of K = 4 is inserted. The potential difference becomes
quiz.explain: Q is fixed and C becomes 4C, so V = Q/C becomes V/4.
quiz.mistake: Treats V as fixed when the battery is disconnected

quiz.q: What area (in units of 10⁹ m²) would a 1 F air-filled parallel plate capacitor with a 1 cm gap need? (ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²; give to 2 decimal places)
quiz.explain: A = Cd/ε₀ = 1 × 0.01/8.85 × 10⁻¹² ≈ 1.13 × 10⁹ m². This shows the farad is a huge unit.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by ε₀ instead of dividing

quiz.q: The dielectric constant K of a medium is defined as
options: the ratio ε/ε₀ of its permittivity to that of free space
the field inside it divided by applied field
quiz.explain: K = ε/ε₀ is dimensionless and greater than 1.
steps: It is dimensionless and greater than 1
Answer: the ratio ε/ε₀ of its permittivity to that of free space

quiz.q: With charge held fixed, inserting a dielectric of constant K into a capacitor makes the field between the plates
quiz.explain: Polarisation reduces the field by a factor K.
steps: Polarisation reduces the field by the factor K
quiz.mistake: Thinks the dielectric increases the field

quiz.q: Which material listed would give the largest capacitance when filling the same capacitor?
quiz.explain: Water has K ≈ 80, much larger than mica (≈ 6) and air (≈ 1).
steps: C = Kε₀A/d, so larger K gives larger C
quiz.mistake: Assumes solids always have larger K

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How can I make my capacitor store more charge at the same voltage?'
teach.praise: Chirp! C = Kε₀A/d: bigger plates, smaller gap, or a dielectric with large K. More charge for the same volts!
teach.nudge: Good! What three things in C = Kε₀A/d could you change?

revise.summary: For a parallel plate capacitor C = ε₀A/d; one farad needs an enormous area. A dielectric of constant K = ε/ε₀ filling the gap multiplies C by K and, at fixed charge, divides E and V by K.
focus: Effect of a dielectric at fixed charge

learn.hook: An Indian electronics hobbyist with only 2 µF capacitors can still make 1 µF, 3 µF or 4 µF. The trick is combining them in series and parallel.
points: Series: each capacitor carries the same charge Q; voltages add. 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ + ... (C is less than the smallest).
Parallel: each capacitor has the same voltage V; charges add. C = C₁ + C₂ + ... (C is more than the largest).
Two in series: C = C₁C₂/(C₁ + C₂). n equal capacitors C: series gives C/n, parallel gives nC.
Slab of thickness t (< d) with constant K: C = ε₀A/(d - t + t/K). A metal slab (K → ∞) gives C = ε₀A/(d - t).
To build a required C and voltage rating, put capacitors in series to share the voltage, and parallel rows to increase C.

learn.hook: Defibrillators in Indian ambulances store around 200 J in a capacitor and dump it into a patient's heart in milliseconds to restore its rhythm.
points: Energy stored: U = Q²/2C = ½CV² = ½QV. It is the work done in charging the capacitor.
The energy is stored in the electric field between the plates, with energy density u = ½ε₀E² (per unit volume). With a dielectric, u = ½Kε₀E².

Connecting a charged capacitor to an uncharged one: charge is shared until both reach a common potential V = (C₁V₁ + C₂V₂)/(C₁ + C₂). Some energy is always lost as heat and radiation in the connecting wires.
Dielectric inserted with battery connected: V fixed, C → KC, Q → KQ, U → KU.
Dielectric inserted after disconnecting: Q fixed, C → KC, V → V/K, U → U/K.

learn.hook: Electrostatics froze charges in place. Now let them flow, and you get everything from a lightning bolt to the UPI payment pinging on your phone.
points: Moving charges make an electric current. Examples: lightning in a thunderstorm, electrons in battery circuits, ions in electrolytes and in our nerves.
Current I = rate of flow of charge. Steady current: I = q/t. In general I(t) = dq/dt, the limit of Δq/Δt.
SI unit: ampere (A), a base unit; 1 A = 1 C s⁻¹. Smaller units: mA (10⁻³ A) and µA (10⁻⁶ A).
Conventional current is the direction of flow of positive charge, so it is opposite to the flow of electrons.
Typical sizes: household appliances draw a few amperes, nerve signals involve microamperes, while lightning can carry tens of thousands of amperes.

topics.title: Charge flow in conductors and Ohm's law

learn.hook: Inside a copper wire, electrons zip around at about 10⁶ m s⁻¹, yet without a battery no current flows. Why? Their motion is random.
points: Charge carriers: free electrons in metals; positive and negative ions in electrolytes.
With no field, free electrons move randomly in all directions, so the net flow through any cross-section is zero.
A field applied across the conductor gives electrons a small net drift, producing a current. A cell or other source is needed to keep the field going, or charges would pile up and cancel it.
Ohm's law: for a metallic conductor at constant temperature, V ∝ I, so V = IR. R is the resistance, unit ohm (Ω), 1 Ω = 1 V A⁻¹.
A graph of V against I for an ohmic conductor is a straight line through the origin; its slope is R.

example.q: A 12 V source drives 0.4 A through a resistor. Find R and the current if V is raised to 18 V (same temperature).

learn.reallife: An electrician testing a geyser element in a Pune flat uses a multimeter: measuring V and I and dividing gives R, exactly Ohm's law.
