learn.hook: Why are Indian Railways' overhead lines thick copper alloy, while a geyser element is thin nichrome? It comes down to R = ρl/A.
points: R = ρl/A: resistance is proportional to length l and inversely proportional to cross-sectional area A.
Resistivity ρ is a property of the material (and temperature), not of the shape. Unit: Ω m. Copper has ρ ≈ 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m.
Conductivity σ = 1/ρ, unit S m⁻¹ (siemens per metre) or Ω⁻¹ m⁻¹.
Current density j = I/A (A m⁻²), and Ohm's law in vector form is j = σE.
Stretching a wire keeps its volume constant: if length becomes n times, area becomes 1/n times, so R becomes n² times.

example.q: A wire of resistance 4 Ω is stretched to twice its length. Find the new resistance.
steps: Volume is constant: l → 2l, A → A/2

topics.title: Drift velocity and the origin of resistance

learn.hook: Electrons in your house wiring crawl at less than a millimetre per second, yet the bulb lights the instant you flip the switch. Both facts are true at once.
points: In a field E, each free electron accelerates (a = -eE/m) between collisions; the average time between collisions is the relaxation time τ.
Drift velocity: vd = -eEτ/m, the average velocity of electrons, opposite to E.
Current I = neAvd, where n is the number density of free electrons and A is the cross-section.
Combining, j = (ne²τ/m)E, so ρ = m/(ne²τ). Resistance arises from collisions.
vd is tiny (about 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹), but the field travels along the wire nearly at the speed of light, so all electrons start drifting almost at once.

example.q: A copper wire (n = 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³) of cross-section 10⁻⁶ m² carries 1.36 A. Find vd.

learn.reallife: An Indian Railways signal kilometres away responds instantly when the cabin switch is thrown, even though electrons in the cable barely creep. The field, not the individual electron, carries the signal.

learn.hook: Ohm's law is not a law of nature like gravity; it is a rule many materials obey. Diodes, LEDs and even a hot bulb filament break it.
points: Mobility µ = |vd|/E = eτ/m: drift speed per unit field. SI unit: m² V⁻¹ s⁻¹.
Non-ohmic case 1: the V-I graph is not a straight line, for example a bulb filament whose resistance rises as it heats up at high currents.
Non-ohmic case 2: the relation depends on the sign of V, as in a diode, which conducts much more in one direction.
Non-ohmic case 3: more than one value of V for the same I, as shown by GaAs-type materials.
For non-ohmic devices, V/I is not constant, so a single resistance value does not describe them.

topics.title: Resistivity of materials and its temperature dependence

learn.hook: From silver to quartz, resistivities span more than 20 orders of magnitude, the biggest range of any common physical property.
points: Materials are classified by resistivity: conductors (metals, about 10⁻⁸ to 10⁻⁶ Ω m), semiconductors (in between) and insulators (up to 10¹⁴ Ω m or more).
The range covers more than 20 orders of magnitude.
For metals, ρ rises with temperature: ρT = ρ₀[1 + α(T - T₀)], where α is the temperature coefficient of resistivity (unit K⁻¹ or °C⁻¹).
For metals α is positive. Alloys like manganin and constantan have very small α, so they are used for standard resistors.
Nichrome has high ρ and small α, so it is used in heating elements.

learn.reallife: Standard resistors at India's National Physical Laboratory in New Delhi are made from alloys like manganin, whose resistance barely changes with room temperature.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why does a metal wire resist more when it gets hot?'
teach.praise: Chirp! For metals, resistivity rises with temperature: ρ = ρ₀[1 + α(T - T₀)] with positive α. Nice!
teach.nudge: Good! How does the resistivity of a metal depend on temperature?

revise.summary: Resistivity ranges from about 10⁻⁸ Ω m for metals to 10¹⁴ Ω m for insulators, with semiconductors between. For metals ρ rises with temperature as ρT = ρ₀[1 + α(T − T₀)]; manganin and constantan have tiny α and nichrome suits heaters.
remember: Manganin, constantan: tiny α (standard resistors); nichrome: high ρ, small α (heaters)
traps: Use T − T₀, not T alone
Semiconductors' resistivity does not behave like metals'

learn.hook: Heat a copper wire and it resists more. Heat a silicon chip and it conducts better. One formula, ρ = m/(ne²τ), explains both.
points: Semiconductors and insulators: resistivity decreases as temperature rises (negative α).
Using ρ = m/(ne²τ): in metals, n is nearly constant, but hotter ions vibrate more, collisions are more frequent, τ falls, so ρ rises.
In semiconductors, extra heat frees many more charge carriers; the rise in n outweighs the fall in τ, so ρ falls.
Finding the temperature of a heating element: from R and R₀ and α, use T = T₀ + (R - R₀)/(R₀α).
This principle is used in resistance thermometers and in thermistors.

revise.summary: In metals n is fixed and hotter ions shorten τ, so resistivity rises; in semiconductors and insulators heat frees many carriers, so resistivity falls. The hot temperature of an element follows from T = T₀ + (R − R₀)/(R₀α).

learn.hook: Your electricity bill counts kilowatt-hours, and every one of them comes from charges falling through potential differences, warming wires on the way.
points: When charge q moves through potential difference V, energy qV is delivered. Power P = VI.
For a resistor, P = VI = I²R = V²/R. This energy appears as heat (Joule heating).
Transmission lines lose power I²Rc in their resistance Rc.
To deliver power P at voltage V, I = P/V, so loss = P²Rc/V². Raising V greatly reduces the loss.
That is why power is sent at very high voltages (hundreds of kV) and stepped down near homes.

example.q: A 1000 W heater runs on 220 V. Find the current and resistance.

learn.reallife: POWERGRID runs 765 kV lines across India so that the current, and hence I²R loss, stays small over thousands of kilometres.

learn.hook: Why does a car's headlight dim when you crank the starter? The battery's own internal resistance steals voltage when a big current flows.
points: An electrolytic cell has two electrodes in an electrolyte. Its emf ε is the potential difference between its terminals when no current flows.
Every cell has an internal resistance r due to its electrolyte.
With current I drawn through an external resistor R: I = ε/(R + r) and terminal voltage V = ε - Ir = IR.
Terminal voltage is less than ε while the cell is delivering current. Maximum current, on short circuit (R = 0), is ε/r.
Emf is not a force; it is energy supplied per unit charge by the cell (unit: volt).

example.q: A cell of emf 2 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω is connected to a 3.5 Ω resistor. Find I and V.

learn.reallife: Inverter batteries in Indian homes are rated by emf (12 V) and must have low internal resistance so their voltage does not sag badly when the fridge or fan draws current during a power cut.

topics.title: Cells in series and in parallel

learn.hook: A torch uses cells in series for more voltage. Solar panel farms in Rajasthan combine panels in series and parallel to get both voltage and current.
points: Two cells in series (positive of one to negative of the other): ε_eq = ε₁ + ε₂ and r_eq = r₁ + r₂. If one cell is reversed, ε_eq = ε₁ - ε₂ while r_eq still adds.
Two cells in parallel: ε_eq = (ε₁r₂ + ε₂r₁)/(r₁ + r₂) and 1/r_eq = 1/r₁ + 1/r₂.
n identical cells (ε, r) in series: emf nε, resistance nr. m identical cells in parallel: emf ε, resistance r/m.
Mixed grouping (m parallel rows, each of n cells in series): ε_eq = nε and r_eq = nr/m; current I = nε/(R + nr/m).
Series increases voltage; parallel lowers internal resistance and lets more current be drawn.

example.q: Two cells of emf 2 V and 1 V with internal resistances 1 Ω and 2 Ω are joined in parallel. Find ε_eq and r_eq.

learn.reallife: Electric rickshaws on Indian streets typically use four 12 V batteries in series, giving 48 V to drive the motor.

Identical cells in parallel have the same emf as a single cell.
ε_eq = ε for identical cells.
Parallel grouping increases the internal resistance.
It decreases it to r/m.
Two parallel cells with ε₁ ≠ ε₂ have an emf between ε₁ and ε₂.
ε_eq is a weighted average.

teach.ask: Gappu has many cells and asks: 'How do I get more voltage? And how do I get more current?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Series adds the emfs for more voltage; parallel lowers internal resistance for more current. Power up!
teach.nudge: Good! Which grouping adds the emfs, and which reduces the internal resistance?

revise.summary: Cells in series add emfs (or subtract if reversed) and internal resistances. In parallel ε_eq = (ε₁r₂ + ε₂r₁)/(r₁ + r₂) and 1/r_eq = 1/r₁ + 1/r₂; m rows of n cells give nε and nr/m.
remember: Series: ε = ε₁ ± ε₂; r = r₁ + r₂
Parallel: ε = (ε₁r₂ + ε₂r₁)/(r₁ + r₂); r = r₁r₂/(r₁ + r₂)
Mixed: ε = nε, r = nr/m; I = nε/(R + nr/m)
traps: Don't subtract r for a reversed cell; only its emf subtracts
Identical cells in parallel do not add emfs; the emf stays ε

learn.hook: Some circuits cannot be reduced to simple series and parallel parts. Gustav Kirchhoff gave two rules that crack any network, from a torch to the national grid.
points: Junction rule: at any junction, the sum of currents entering equals the sum of currents leaving. This is conservation of charge.
Loop rule: the algebraic sum of changes in potential around any closed loop is zero. This is conservation of energy.
Sign convention: going across a resistor in the direction of the assumed current, the potential drops (-IR); against it, it rises (+IR). Going from - to + terminal of a cell, potential rises (+ε).
If a current comes out negative, it simply flows opposite to the direction assumed.
Symmetry helps: in a cube of 12 equal resistors R, the resistance between opposite corners is 5R/6.

example.q: At a junction, 3 A and 2 A flow in along two wires, and 1.5 A flows out along a third. What flows in the fourth wire?
steps: Sum out must also be 5 A
example.answer: 3.5 A flowing out of the junction

learn.reallife: Power engineers at India's National Load Despatch Centre use network equations based on Kirchhoff's rules to balance power flows between regional grids every minute.

Apply the loop rule with sign conventions
Solve the equations and interpret signs

quiz.q: At a junction, currents of 4 A and 3 A enter and a current of 5 A leaves along one wire. What current leaves through the only other wire (in A)?
quiz.explain: In = out: 4 + 3 = 5 + I, so I = 2 A.
steps: Junction rule: total in = total out

quiz.q: Kirchhoff's loop rule is a consequence of
quiz.explain: A charge that goes round a loop returns to the same potential, so no net energy is gained or lost.
steps: Round a closed loop a charge returns to the same potential
No net energy is gained or lost: conservation of energy

quiz.q: In a loop, you go across a 4 Ω resistor in the direction opposite to its current of 2 A. The change in potential is (in V)
quiz.explain: Going against the current, potential rises by IR = +8 V.
steps: Crossing a resistor against the current, potential rises

quiz.q: A single loop has a 10 V cell (negligible r) and resistors of 2 Ω and 3 Ω in series. Using the loop rule, what is the current (in A)?
A loop contains a 12 V cell and a 4 V cell connected to oppose each other, with a total resistance of 4 Ω (including internal resistances). What is the current (in A)?
quiz.explain: Net emf = 12 - 4 = 8 V. I = 8/4 = 2 A, in the direction driven by the 12 V cell.

quiz.q: While solving a network, a current comes out as -0.5 A. This means
options: the current is 0.5 A but flows opposite to the direction assumed
quiz.explain: The assumed direction was just a guess; the sign corrects it.
steps: The direction of current was only assumed
A negative result means it actually flows the other way
Answer: the current is 0.5 A but flows opposite to the direction assumed
quiz.mistake: Thinks a negative current is impossible

quiz.q: Twelve equal resistors of 6 Ω form the edges of a cube. What is the equivalent resistance between two diagonally opposite corners (in Ω)?
quiz.explain: R_eq = 5R/6 = 5 × 6/6 = 5 Ω (by symmetry: current I splits into 3, then 6, then 3 parts).
steps: By symmetry I splits into I/3, then I/6, then I/3
quiz.mistake: Forgets the symmetric splitting of current

quiz.q: Kirchhoff's junction rule is based on
quiz.explain: Charge cannot pile up at a junction in steady state.
steps: Charge cannot pile up at a junction in steady state
So current in = current out: conservation of charge

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What are the two Kirchhoff rules, and why are they true?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Junction rule: current in = out (charge conservation). Loop rule: potential changes add to zero (energy conservation). Woohoo!
teach.nudge: Good! What does each rule say, and which conservation law is behind it?

revise.summary: Kirchhoff's junction rule (charge conservation) says current in equals current out; the loop rule (energy conservation) says potential changes round a loop sum to zero. Careful sign conventions and symmetry solve networks.
focus: Interpreting negative currents; cube of resistors
remember: Across R with current: −IR; against: +IR; cell − to +: +ε
Cube of 12 R across body diagonal: 5R/6
traps: A negative current is not an error; it only means the current flows opposite to the direction assumed
Don't mix them up: the loop rule is energy conservation, the junction rule is charge conservation

learn.hook: Before digital meters, the Wheatstone bridge was the gold standard for measuring resistance. It still hides inside weighing scales and strain gauges.
points: Four resistors P, Q, R and S form a diamond ABCD: P from A to B, Q from B to C, R from A to D, S from D to C. A cell is connected across A and C, and a galvanometer across B and D.
Balanced bridge: no current flows through the galvanometer, so B and D are at the same potential.
Applying Kirchhoff's rules with Ig = 0 gives the balance condition P/Q = R/S.
If three resistances are known, the fourth is found from the balance condition: S = RQ/P.
If the bridge is not balanced, a current flows through the galvanometer; it is found using Kirchhoff's rules.

example.q: In a balanced Wheatstone bridge, P = 100 Ω, Q = 10 Ω and R = 30 Ω. Find the unknown S.

learn.reallife: Digital weighing scales at Indian kirana shops use strain gauges in a Wheatstone bridge: the weight slightly changes one arm's resistance, unbalancing the bridge in proportion to the load.

items.text: At balance, the current through the galvanometer is ___.
Balance condition: P/Q = R/___.
At balance, points B and D are at the same ___.
A bridge with Ig ≠ 0 is called ___.

items.q: P = 2 Ω, Q = 4 Ω, R = 3 Ω: S (in Ω)
P = 10 Ω, Q = 10 Ω, R = 7 Ω: S (in Ω)
P = 5 Ω, Q = 1 Ω, R = 20 Ω: S (in Ω)
P = 100 Ω, Q = 50 Ω, R = 40 Ω: S (in Ω)
P = 3 Ω, Q = 9 Ω, R = 2 Ω: S (in Ω)

quiz.q: A Wheatstone bridge balances with P = 8 Ω, Q = 2 Ω and R = 12 Ω. What is S (in Ω)?
quiz.explain: P/Q = R/S gives S = RQ/P = 24/8 = 3 Ω.
quiz.mistake: Inverts the ratio and gets 48 Ω

quiz.q: In a balanced bridge, why does no current flow through the galvanometer?
options: The two ends of the galvanometer are at the same potential
The currents in all four arms are equal
quiz.explain: Current flows only if there is a potential difference across the galvanometer.
steps: In balance, B and D are at the same potential
No potential difference ⇒ no galvanometer current
Answer: The two ends of the galvanometer are at the same potential
quiz.mistake: Thinks balance needs all arms to carry equal current

quiz.q: Four resistors P = 2 Ω, Q = 4 Ω, R = 6 Ω and S = 12 Ω form a bridge. Is it balanced?
options: No, since P + Q ≠ R + S
Only if the cell emf is 6 V
quiz.explain: 2/4 = 6/12 = 0.5, so the bridge is balanced whatever the cell.
steps: They are equal, so the bridge is balanced

quiz.q: In a balanced bridge, the galvanometer and the cell are interchanged. The bridge
quiz.explain: The condition P/Q = R/S is symmetric; swapping cell and galvanometer keeps balance.
steps: Balance condition P/Q = R/S is symmetric
Interchanging cell and galvanometer leaves it satisfied
quiz.mistake: Thinks positions of cell and galvanometer matter for balance

quiz.q: A bridge has P = Q = R = 10 Ω and S = 10 Ω with a galvanometer of 20 Ω. If S is changed to 20 Ω, will a galvanometer current flow?
options: No, because the galvanometer resistance is large
Only if the cell is reversed
quiz.explain: Balance needs P/Q = R/S; now 1 ≠ 1/2, so the bridge is unbalanced.
steps: 1 ≠ 0.5, so the bridge is unbalanced and current flows
quiz.mistake: Thinks P = Q alone ensures balance

quiz.q: In bridge ABCD, P = 1 Ω (A to B), Q = 2 Ω (B to C), R = 2 Ω (A to D) and S = 1 Ω (D to C). A 10 V cell of negligible internal resistance is connected across A and C, and a galvanometer of resistance 2 Ω across B and D. What current flows through the galvanometer (in A)?
quiz.explain: P/Q = 1/2 but R/S = 2, so the bridge is unbalanced. Taking V_C = 0 and V_A = 10 V, the junction rule at B and D gives V_B = 6 V and V_D = 4 V, so Ig = (6 - 4)/2 = 1 A, from B to D.
quiz.mistake: Assumes the galvanometer current is zero without checking the balance condition

quiz.q: When a bridge is balanced, the galvanometer can be removed without changing any current. Why?
options: Because it is in series with the cell
It carries zero current, so removing it changes nothing
quiz.explain: A branch with zero current can be removed (or replaced by any resistor) without effect.
steps: At balance the galvanometer branch carries zero current
Removing a zero-current branch changes nothing
Answer: It carries zero current, so removing it changes nothing
quiz.mistake: Thinks every branch affects the network

quiz.q: In a balanced bridge P = 4 Ω, Q = 6 Ω and S = 9 Ω. What is R (in Ω)?
A wire of resistance 8 Ω is used as S in a balanced bridge with P = 2 Ω and Q = 4 Ω. What is R (in Ω)?

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What is so special about a balanced Wheatstone bridge?'
teach.praise: Chirp! At balance the galvanometer shows zero current because its ends are at the same potential, and P/Q = R/S. Bridge mastered!
teach.nudge: Good! What does the galvanometer show at balance, and what condition holds?

revise.summary: A Wheatstone bridge has four resistors with a cell and a galvanometer across opposite corners. At balance no galvanometer current flows and P/Q = R/S, giving an unknown resistance; otherwise Kirchhoff's rules find the current.
remember: At balance the galvanometer branch can be removed
traps: Don't compare the ratios in the wrong order; match P/Q with R/S
Swapping the cell and galvanometer does not upset the balance

learn.hook: In 1820, during a lecture demonstration, Hans Christian Oersted saw a compass needle twitch near a current-carrying wire. Electricity and magnetism were joined for good.
points: Oersted's discovery (1820): a current in a straight wire deflects a nearby compass needle. The needle sets along circles around the wire.
Moving charges (currents) produce magnetic fields. Reversing the current reverses the deflection.
Later, Maxwell unified electricity and magnetism and showed light is an electromagnetic wave.
Notation: a dot ⊙ means a field or current coming out of the page (towards you); a cross ⊗ means going into the page.
Magnetic fields obey superposition: the field of several sources is the vector sum of their individual fields. Like E, B is a vector field.

example.q: A compass is placed just below a wire running north-south. When the current flows north, the needle's north pole swings west. What happens if the current is reversed?
steps: Below a wire carrying current northwards, the field points west (right-hand thumb rule), so the north pole swings west.
Reversing the current reverses the field around the wire.
The force on the needle's poles reverses, so it swings the other way.
example.answer: The north pole now swings east

learn.reallife: Railway engineers keep sensitive magnetic compasses and instruments away from heavy-current traction cables on electrified Indian Railways routes, because the current's magnetic field can deflect them.

games.title: Oersted's lessons
items: A steady current in a wire produces a magnetic field around it.
That was Oersted's observation.
A stationary charge produces a magnetic field.
Only moving charges (currents) do.
The symbol ⊗ means a field directed into the page.
Think of the tail feathers of an arrow going away.
Magnetic fields from two sources add as vectors.
Superposition holds for B.
Reversing the current leaves the compass deflection unchanged.
The deflection reverses.

quiz.q: Who first observed that an electric current deflects a magnetic compass needle?
quiz.explain: Oersted noticed this in 1820, linking electricity and magnetism.
steps: In 1820 a current in a wire was seen to deflect a nearby compass
This was observed by Hans Christian Oersted
quiz.mistake: Credits Faraday, who later discovered induction

quiz.q: In a diagram, a magnetic field pointing straight towards the reader is shown by
quiz.explain: A dot is like the tip of an arrow coming at you.
steps: A dot ⊙ is like the tip of an arrow coming at you
A cross ⊗ means going into the page
quiz.mistake: Swaps the dot and cross conventions

quiz.q: A compass placed near a straight wire with current tends to align
options: along circles centred on the wire
quiz.explain: The field of a straight wire forms concentric circles around it.
steps: The field of a straight current forms concentric circles around the wire
The needle lines up along these circles
Answer: along circles centred on the wire
quiz.mistake: Thinks the field is along the wire

quiz.q: Which of these produces a magnetic field?
options: A charged comb kept on a table
A neutral atom at rest with no magnetic moment
quiz.explain: Moving charges make magnetic fields; static charges make only electric fields.
steps: Only moving charges produce magnetic fields
Charges at rest give only electric fields
Answer: An electron moving through space
quiz.mistake: Thinks any charge makes a magnetic field

quiz.q: Two wires each produce a field of 3 µT at a point, in the same direction. What is the net field there (in µT)?
quiz.explain: Superposition: same direction, so the fields add: 3 + 3 = 6 µT.

quiz.q: Two wires produce fields of 3 µT (east) and 4 µT (north) at a point. What is the magnitude of the net field (in µT)?
quiz.explain: Fields add as vectors: √(3² + 4²) = 5 µT.

quiz.q: Maxwell's work showed that
options: electricity and magnetism are unified, and light is an electromagnetic wave
currents do not produce magnetic fields
light is a stream of electrons
quiz.explain: Maxwell's equations predicted EM waves moving at the speed of light.
steps: His theory showed light is an electromagnetic wave
Answer: electricity and magnetism are unified, and light is an electromagnetic wave

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A compass needle deflects near a wire only while current flows. Reason (R): Only moving charges produce magnetic fields. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
quiz.explain: When the current stops, the charges no longer drift, so there is no magnetic field to turn the needle.
steps: A: the needle deflects only while current flows – true
R: only moving charges produce magnetic fields – true
No current ⇒ no moving charges ⇒ no field; R explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Does not link the field to the motion of charges

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why does my compass go crazy near a wire with current?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Moving charges in the wire make a magnetic field around it, which turns the compass. Thanks, Oersted!
teach.nudge: Good! What does a current produce around it?

revise.summary: Oersted (1820) found that a current deflects a compass, showing moving charges make magnetic fields, which form circles around a straight wire. Magnetic fields add by superposition, and Maxwell unified electricity and magnetism.
remember: B is a vector; fields add as vectors
traps: Static charges make no magnetic field
Perpendicular fields add by Pythagoras, not arithmetic

topics.title: Lorentz force on a moving charge

learn.hook: Charged particles from the Sun are steered by Earth's magnetic field into the polar skies, painting the auroras. The steering force is the Lorentz force.
points: Lorentz force: F = q[E + v × B]. The magnetic part is F = q(v × B), magnitude qvB sinθ.
The magnetic force is perpendicular to both v and B. It is zero if the charge is at rest or moves along B (θ = 0 or 180°).
Direction: use the right-hand rule for v × B (fingers along v, curl towards B, thumb gives the force on a positive charge). Reverse it for a negative charge.
SI unit of B: tesla (T), where 1 T = 1 N s C⁻¹ m⁻¹ = 1 N A⁻¹ m⁻¹. Smaller unit: gauss, 1 G = 10⁻⁴ T.
Typical fields: Earth's surface about 10⁻⁵ T; a lab magnet about 1 T; a neutron star about 10⁸ T.

example.q: A proton moves at 2 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a 0.5 T field. Find the force on it.
example.answer: 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ N, perpendicular to both v and B

learn.reallife: Auroras are rarely seen from India, but ISRO's Aditya-L1 solar observatory studies the solar wind whose charged particles feel the Lorentz force as they reach Earth's magnetic field.

games.title: Lorentz force check
items: The magnetic force on a charge at rest is zero.
v = 0 means qv × B = 0.
A charge moving parallel to B feels the maximum magnetic force.
sin 0° = 0, so the force is zero.
The magnetic force on a moving charge is perpendicular to its velocity.
It comes from a cross product with v.
1 gauss = 10⁻⁴ tesla.
So Earth's ~0.5 G field is ~5 × 10⁻⁵ T.
An electron and a proton moving the same way in the same field feel forces in the same direction.
Opposite charges get opposite forces.

quiz.q: An electron moves at 3 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ at right angles to a field of 0.2 T. What is the magnitude of the force on it (in units of 10⁻¹⁴ N)? (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
quiz.mistake: Slips by a power of ten

quiz.q: A charge of 2 µC moves at 10⁴ m s⁻¹ at 30° to a field of 0.5 T. What is the magnetic force (in mN)?
A proton moves along +x in a field along +y. What is the direction of the magnetic force on it?
quiz.explain: F = q(v × B) = e(x̂ × ŷ) = +eẑ.
steps: v along x̂, B along ŷ: x̂ × ŷ = ẑ
quiz.mistake: Uses the left-hand order or forgets the cross product

quiz.q: An electron moves along +x in a field along +y. The magnetic force on it points along
quiz.explain: x̂ × ŷ = ẑ, and the negative charge flips it to -z.
steps: x̂ × ŷ = ẑ for a positive charge
An electron is negative, so the force reverses
quiz.mistake: Forgets to reverse the direction for a negative charge

quiz.q: A charged particle moves through a region with no deflection. Which conclusion is certain?
options: It cannot be concluded that B = 0, since the particle may be moving along B
The particle must be at rest
quiz.explain: A charge moving parallel to B feels no magnetic force, so the field could be non-zero.
steps: Magnetic force = qvB sinθ is zero if v is parallel to B
So no deflection does not prove B = 0
Answer: It cannot be concluded that B = 0, since the particle may be moving along B
quiz.mistake: Assumes no deflection always means no field

quiz.q: Why does the magnetic force not change the speed of a charge?
options: It is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work
It acts only on charges at rest
It is parallel to the velocity
quiz.explain: A force perpendicular to motion changes direction but not kinetic energy.
steps: F = q(v × B) is always perpendicular to v
A perpendicular force does no work, so kinetic energy (speed) is unchanged
Answer: It is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work
quiz.mistake: Thinks any force must change the speed

quiz.q: Which is the SI unit of magnetic field?
quiz.explain: The tesla (T) is the SI unit; the gauss is a smaller non-SI unit.
steps: SI unit of B: tesla (1 T = 1 N A⁻¹ m⁻¹)
The gauss (10⁻⁴ T) is not SI

quiz.q: The Lorentz force on a charge q in combined fields is
quiz.explain: Electric force qE plus magnetic force q(v × B).
steps: Electric force qE + magnetic force q(v × B)
Lorentz force F = q(E + v × B)
quiz.mistake: Mixes up which field the velocity multiplies

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If a magnetic field pushes a moving charge, why doesn't the charge speed up?'
teach.praise: Chirp! The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work. It only turns the charge!
teach.nudge: Good! What is the angle between the magnetic force and the velocity?

revise.summary: A charge in E and B feels the Lorentz force F = q(E + v × B); the magnetic part qvB sinθ is perpendicular to v and B and does no work. B is measured in tesla (1 G = 10⁻⁴ T).
focus: Magnitude and direction of magnetic force
When the magnetic force is zero
remember: Zero if v = 0 or v ∥ B
1 T = 1 N A⁻¹ m⁻¹; 1 G = 10⁻⁴ T
traps: Don't forget to reverse the force direction for negative charges
No deflection does not prove B = 0

learn.hook: Every electric motor, from a ceiling fan to an electric scooter, works because a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field gets a push.
points: A straight conductor of length l carrying current I in a uniform field B feels F = I l × B, magnitude BIl sinθ.
This is just the sum of Lorentz forces on the drifting electrons in the wire.
Direction: l points along the current; use the right-hand rule (or Fleming's left-hand rule).
A horizontal wire can float if the magnetic force balances its weight: BIl = mg.
On individual charges, the magnetic force does no work, so their speed stays constant.

example.q: A 0.2 m wire of mass 20 g lies horizontally in a horizontal field of 0.5 T perpendicular to it. What current makes it float? (g = 9.8 m s⁻²)

learn.reallife: Loudspeakers in a Bollywood cinema hall use a coil in a magnet's field. The force BIl on the coil changes with the audio current and moves the speaker cone.

items.q: Wire parallel to B: F (in N)

The force on a wire is along the direction of the current.

F ∝ I.

It does no work on them.

quiz.q: A wire 0.5 m long carries 4 A at right angles to a field of 0.3 T. What force acts on it (in N)?
A 10 cm wire carries 5 A at 30° to a 0.8 T field. What is the force on it (in N)?

A horizontal wire carries current towards the north in a magnetic field pointing vertically upward. In which direction is the force on the wire?
quiz.explain: F = I l × B. Taking x = east, y = north and z = up: ŷ × ẑ = x̂, so the force points east.
steps: F = I l × B; take x = east, y = north, z = up
l along ŷ, B along ẑ: ŷ × ẑ = x̂
quiz.mistake: Reverses the order of the cross product and gets west

quiz.q: Why does a magnetic field do no work on the charges in a wire, even though the wire itself can be pushed?
options: Work is done only on protons
The force on each charge is perpendicular to its velocity
quiz.explain: Each charge's magnetic force is perpendicular to its motion, so no work is done on it directly.
steps: Each charge feels q(v × B), perpendicular to its own velocity
So no work is done on any individual charge
Answer: The force on each charge is perpendicular to its velocity
quiz.mistake: Thinks the magnetic field directly supplies the energy

quiz.q: The force on a straight conductor in a uniform field is given by
quiz.explain: F = I l × B, with l along the current.
steps: Sum of Lorentz forces on drifting charges
F = I l × B, with l along the current
quiz.mistake: Reverses the cross product or uses a dot product

quiz.q: The current in a wire is doubled and the field is halved. The force on the wire
Assertion (A): A current-carrying wire placed along a magnetic field feels no force. Reason (R): The force on a wire is BIl sinθ, and θ = 0 here. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: sin 0° = 0, so the force vanishes when the wire is parallel to B.
steps: A: a wire along B feels no force – true
R: F = BIl sinθ with θ = 0 – true
sin0° = 0 gives zero force, so R explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Does not apply the sinθ factor

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How does a motor get its push from a magnet?'
teach.praise: Chirp! A current-carrying wire in a magnetic field feels F = BIl sinθ, which pushes the coil round. Vroom!
teach.nudge: Good! What force acts on a wire carrying current in a magnetic field?

revise.summary: A straight wire of length l carrying I in a uniform field B feels F = I l × B, magnitude BIl sinθ, the sum of Lorentz forces on its electrons. A wire floats when BIl = mg.
focus: Direction of force on a wire
remember: F = I l × B; |F| = BIl sinθ
Zero when the wire is along B
traps: l does not point along the electron flow; it points along the current
The field does no work on individual charges

topics.title: Circular and helical motion in a magnetic field

learn.hook: Particle accelerators and mass spectrometers bend charged particles into circles with magnets. The radius tells you the particle's momentum.
points: A charge moving perpendicular to a uniform B moves in a circle: qvB = mv²/r, so r = mv/(qB) = p/(qB).
Angular frequency ω = qB/m; frequency ν = qB/(2πm); period T = 2πm/(qB). These do not depend on speed or radius (cyclotron frequency).
If v has a component v∥ along B, that part is unaffected, while v⊥ makes the circle: the path is a helix.
Pitch of the helix = distance moved along B in one revolution = v∥T = 2πm v∥/(qB). Radius r = mv⊥/(qB).
Faster particles make bigger circles but take the same time per revolution.

example.q: An electron moves at 4 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a field of 9.1 × 10⁻⁴ T. Find the radius of its path. (mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)

learn.reallife: Mass spectrometers at BARC, Mumbai, separate isotopes by bending ions in a magnetic field: heavier ions of the same charge and speed curve along larger radii.

games.title: Circling charges
items: The period of a charge circling in a uniform B depends on its speed.
T = 2πm/(qB) has no v.
Doubling the speed doubles the radius.
r ∝ v.
A charge entering at an angle to B follows a helix.
v∥ is unchanged while v⊥ circles.
The kinetic energy of the circling charge increases each revolution.
Magnetic force does no work.
A heavier ion with the same charge and speed moves on a larger circle.
r ∝ m.

quiz.q: A proton (m = 1.6 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) moves at 10⁶ m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a field of 0.1 T. What is the radius of its circular path (in cm)? (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
quiz.mistake: Slips by a power of ten

quiz.q: The speed of a charged particle moving in a circle in a uniform magnetic field is doubled. Its period of revolution
quiz.explain: T = 2πm/(qB) is independent of speed.
steps: It has no v in it
quiz.mistake: Thinks a faster particle must finish the circle sooner

quiz.q: A charged particle moving in a circle in a field B has radius 4 cm. If B is doubled (same speed), the radius becomes (in cm)
quiz.explain: r = mv/(qB) ∝ 1/B, so r halves.

quiz.q: A particle with v∥ = 3 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ along B has a period of 2 × 10⁻⁶ s for its circular part. What is the pitch of its helix (in m)?
quiz.mistake: Uses the perpendicular component instead of the parallel one

quiz.q: Which expression gives the angular frequency of a charge in a uniform magnetic field?
quiz.explain: From qvB = mω²r and v = ωr: ω = qB/m.

quiz.q: An alpha particle (charge 2e, mass 4m) and a proton (charge e, mass m) enter the same field with the same speed, perpendicular to B. What is r(alpha)/r(proton)?
steps: r = mv/(qB); same v and B
quiz.mistake: Ignores the charge of the alpha particle

quiz.q: A charged particle enters a uniform magnetic field at 60° to B. Its path will be
options: a helix with its axis along B
a circle in a plane containing B
quiz.explain: The component along B is unchanged; the perpendicular component gives circular motion. Together, a helix.
steps: v∥ (along B) is unchanged; v⊥ gives a circle
Circle + steady drift along B = helix with axis along B
Answer: a helix with its axis along B

quiz.q: An electron and a proton enter a uniform field perpendicularly with the same momentum. Which statement is correct?
options: The electron's circle is much bigger
The proton's circle is much bigger
They move on circles of the same radius but in opposite senses
quiz.explain: r = p/(qB) is the same for equal p and |q|, but opposite charges curve in opposite directions.
steps: r = p/(qB); same p and same |q| ⇒ same r
Opposite signs make them curve in opposite senses
Answer: They move on circles of the same radius but in opposite senses
quiz.mistake: Thinks the lighter particle always curves more

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If a charge goes faster in a magnetic field, does it go round quicker?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Faster means a bigger circle, but the period 2πm/(qB) stays the same. Tricky!
teach.nudge: Good! How do the radius and the period depend on speed?

revise.summary: A charge moving perpendicular to uniform B moves in a circle of radius r = mv/(qB) with ω = qB/m and period T = 2πm/(qB), independent of speed. With a component along B the path is a helix of pitch v∥T.
focus: Radius, period and frequency of circular motion
traps: Period does not depend on speed or radius
Don't use the full speed for the radius of a helix; use only v⊥

learn.hook: Coulomb's law gives the field of a point charge. For magnetism there are no magnetic charges, so Biot and Savart built the field from tiny pieces of current instead.
points: Biot-Savart law: dB = (µ₀/4π) I dl × r/r³, magnitude dB = (µ₀/4π) I dl sinθ/r², where θ is between dl and r.
µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹ (permeability of free space), so µ₀/4π = 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹.
Similarities with Coulomb's law: both are inverse-square and long-range, and both obey superposition.
Differences: the source is a vector (I dl) not a scalar charge; dB depends on the angle θ and is perpendicular to both dl and r; dB = 0 along the line of the element.
Remarkably, µ₀ε₀ = 1/c², so c = 1/√(µ₀ε₀) ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

example.q: An element dl = 1 cm carrying 10 A lies along x. Find dB at 0.5 m along y from it.

learn.reallife: Engineers designing MRI machines for Indian hospitals compute the field of every turn of the coils by adding Biot-Savart contributions from tiny current elements.

Answer: perpendicular to the plane containing dl and r

quiz.explain: 1/√(µ₀ε₀) = c, the speed of light.

quiz.explain: dB ∝ 1/r².

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How does a tiny bit of current wire make a magnetic field?'
teach.praise: Chirp! By the Biot-Savart law, dB = (µ₀/4π) I dl sinθ/r². Add all the bits to get the full field!
teach.nudge: Good! Which law gives the field of a small current element, and how does it depend on angle and distance?

revise.summary: The Biot-Savart law gives dB = (µ₀/4π) I dl sinθ/r², perpendicular to both dl and r, with µ₀/4π = 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹. Like Coulomb's law it is inverse-square, but it depends on angle and is zero along the element.
remember: dB = 0 along the line of the element
traps: Don't take θ from any other line; it is the angle between dl and r
Don't use 4π × 10⁻⁷ for µ₀/4π

topics.title: Field of a circular current loop

learn.hook: Coil a wire into a loop and the field at its centre gets concentrated. Wind many loops and you have the coils of motors, speakers and MRI scanners.
points: On the axis of a loop of radius R at distance x from the centre: B = µ₀IR²/[2(x² + R²)^(3/2)], along the axis (from Biot-Savart; the perpendicular parts cancel by symmetry).
At the centre (x = 0): B = µ₀I/(2R). For N turns: B = µ₀NI/(2R).
For an arc subtending angle θ (in radians) at its centre: B = µ₀Iθ/(4πR). A semicircle gives µ₀I/(4R).
Right-hand thumb rule for a loop: curl the fingers along the current, and the thumb points along B through the loop.
Field lines of a loop are like those of a short bar magnet: they come out of one face and go into the other.

example.q: A coil of 200 turns, radius 8 cm, carries 0.5 A. Find B at its centre. (π = 3.14)

learn.reallife: The tangent galvanometer, once common in Indian college labs, uses the field at the centre of a circular coil, µ₀NI/2R, balanced against Earth's horizontal field.

teach.praise: Chirp! Curl the right-hand fingers along the current and the thumb points along B through the loop. Easy!
teach.nudge: Good! Which hand rule do we use, and what do the fingers and thumb represent?

revise.summary: A circular loop gives B = µ₀IR²/[2(x² + R²)^(3/2)] on its axis and µ₀NI/(2R) at its centre; an arc of angle θ gives µ₀Iθ/(4πR). The right-hand thumb rule gives the direction, and the loop behaves like a small bar magnet.
focus: Field at the centre of a coil
traps: Use radius, not diameter
Don't put θ in degrees; it must be in radians

topics.title: Ampere's circuital law and the straight wire

learn.hook: Gauss's law makes symmetric electric problems easy. Ampere's law does the same for magnetic fields of straight wires, cylinders and solenoids.
points: Ampere's circuital law: ∮B·dl = µ₀I, where I is the net current passing through the closed loop (the Amperian loop).
Choose a loop where B is constant and tangent (or normal, so B·dl = 0) by symmetry, just as a Gaussian surface is chosen for Gauss's law.
Long straight wire: a circle of radius r gives B(2πr) = µ₀I, so B = µ₀I/(2πr) = 2 × 10⁻⁷ I/r.
Direction: right-hand thumb rule. Thumb along the current, curled fingers give the circular field lines.
Long solid cylinder of radius a with uniform current I: outside B = µ₀I/(2πr); inside B = µ₀Ir/(2πa²), rising linearly from zero at the axis.

example.q: A long straight wire carries 5 A. Find B at 10 cm.
example.answer: 1 × 10⁻⁵ T, in circles around the wire

learn.reallife: Near a 765 kV transmission line carrying about 1000 A, the field 20 m below is about 10 µT, roughly a fifth of Earth's field. This is what B = µ₀I/(2πr) predicts.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How can I find the magnetic field of a long wire without adding up every tiny bit?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Use Ampere's law with a circular loop: B × 2πr = µ₀I, so B = µ₀I/2πr. Symmetry saves the day!
teach.nudge: Good! Which law and which shape of loop make this easy?

revise.summary: Ampere's circuital law, ∮B·dl = µ₀I_enclosed, uses symmetric loops to find B. A long straight wire gives B = µ₀I/(2πr); a uniform cylinder gives µ₀Ir/(2πa²) inside and µ₀I/(2πr) outside.
focus: Field of a long straight wire
Field inside and outside a cylinder
traps: Don't count currents outside the loop; only enclosed currents count, with signs
Wire field ∝ 1/r, not 1/r²

learn.hook: Wind a wire tightly into a long coil and you can create a strong, uniform magnetic field inside, a magnet you can switch on and off.
points: A long solenoid has a nearly uniform field inside along its axis, and a nearly zero field outside.
Ampere's law with a rectangular loop (one side inside, one outside) gives BL = µ₀(nL)I, so B = µ₀nI, where n = N/L is turns per unit length.
B inside does not depend on the radius or the exact position inside (for a long solenoid).
The solenoid's field resembles a bar magnet's: one end acts as a north pole, the other as a south pole. Use the right-hand rule to find which end is north.
At each end of a long solenoid the field is about half the value inside, µ₀nI/2.

example.q: A solenoid 0.4 m long has 600 turns and carries 2 A. Find B inside. (π = 3.14)

learn.reallife: Electric doorbells and the solenoid valves in Indian washing machines use solenoids: switching on the current magnetises the coil and pulls an iron plunger.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do I make a strong magnetic field I can switch on and off?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Wind a solenoid: B = µ₀nI, so more turns per metre or more current makes it stronger. Switchable magnet!
teach.nudge: Good! Which device does this, and what does its field depend on?

revise.summary: A long solenoid has a nearly uniform field B = µ₀nI inside (n = N/L) and almost none outside, about half that value at its ends. It behaves like a bar magnet with poles fixed by the right-hand rule.
focus: Deriving B = µ₀nI with Ampere's law
Field at the ends and polarity
traps: Use turns per metre, not total turns
A counter-clockwise current (as seen) does not give a south pole facing you; it gives a north pole

learn.hook: Two parallel wires both carrying current towards the same end pull towards each other. That tiny tug was once the official definition of the ampere.
points: Wire a creates B = µ₀Ia/(2πd) at wire b. Force per unit length on b: f = µ₀IaIb/(2πd) = 2 × 10⁻⁷ IaIb/d.
Currents in the same direction (parallel) attract; currents in opposite directions (antiparallel) repel. This is opposite to the rule for like charges.
The forces on the two wires are equal and opposite (Newton's third law).
Historical definition (used until 2019): one ampere is the current which, in two long straight parallel wires 1 m apart in vacuum, produces a force of 2 × 10⁻⁷ N per metre of length.
Since 2019, the ampere is defined by fixing the value of the elementary charge e.

example.q: Two long parallel wires 10 cm apart carry 5 A and 8 A in the same direction. Find the force per metre.

learn.reallife: In large power stations and substations, bus bars carrying thousands of amperes are clamped firmly because the force between parallel currents can bend them during a short-circuit surge.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Two parallel electron beams moving in the same direction in a vacuum repel each other on the whole. Reason (R): Parallel currents attract each other. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

steps: A: same-direction electron beams repel overall – true (electric repulsion is much bigger)

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Two wires with current in the same direction, do they push apart like same charges?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Surprise, parallel currents attract and antiparallel currents repel. The opposite of charges!
teach.nudge: Good! What happens when the currents are in the same direction? And in opposite directions?

revise.summary: Two long parallel wires exert force per unit length f = µ₀IaIb/(2πd) = 2 × 10⁻⁷ IaIb/d on each other, attractive for parallel and repulsive for antiparallel currents. This was the basis of the old ampere definition.
focus: Force per unit length between wires
traps: Don't apply the like-charges rule: parallel currents attract
f is not the total force; multiply by the length to get it

learn.hook: Put a current loop in a magnetic field and it twists. That twist turns the shaft of every DC motor and the needle of every analogue meter.
points: Rectangular loop in a uniform field: the forces on opposite sides cancel, so the net force is zero, but they form a couple.
Torque τ = IAB sinθ for one turn, where θ is between the normal to the loop and B. For N turns: τ = NIAB sinθ.
Vector form: τ = m × B, where the magnetic moment m = NIA (unit A m²), directed along the normal by the right-hand rule.
Stable equilibrium when m is parallel to B (θ = 0); unstable when m is antiparallel (θ = 180°). Torque is zero in both.
Torque is maximum (NIAB) when the plane of the loop is parallel to B (θ = 90°).

example.q: A 100-turn coil of area 0.01 m² carries 2 A in a 0.5 T field, with its plane parallel to B. Find the torque.
steps: Plane parallel to B means θ = 90° between normal and B

learn.reallife: The small DC motors in battery-powered toy cars, cordless drills and car windscreen wipers rely on τ = NIAB sinθ to turn their coils.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why does a current loop turn in a magnetic field but not slide away?'
teach.praise: Chirp! The forces cancel (no net force) but form a couple, giving torque τ = m × B. Twist, no slide!
teach.nudge: Good! What happens to the forces on opposite sides of the loop?

revise.summary: A current loop in a uniform field has zero net force but a torque τ = NIAB sinθ = m × B, with m = NIA along the normal. It is stable when m is along B and torque is maximum when the loop's plane is parallel to B.
remember: τ = NIAB sinθ (θ between normal and B)
m = NIA (A m²); τ = m × B
Stable: m ∥ B; unstable: m antiparallel
traps: Plane parallel to B does not mean θ = 0; it means θ = 90° (maximum torque)
Don't use areas in cm²; convert to m²

topics.title: A current loop as a magnetic dipole

learn.hook: A tiny current loop behaves exactly like a tiny bar magnet. In fact, the magnetism of atoms comes from electrons looping around nuclei.
points: Far along the axis (x ≫ R), a loop's field is B = µ₀m/(2πx³) = (µ₀/4π)(2m/x³), where m = IA.
Compare the electric dipole: E = (1/4πε₀)(2p/x³). Swap p → m and 1/ε₀ → µ₀.
A current loop is a magnetic dipole, with north and south faces.
Unlike electric charges, there are no isolated magnetic charges (monopoles): the simplest magnetic element is the current loop (dipole).

learn.hook: The swinging needle of an old-school analogue meter is a coil, a magnet and a tiny spring working together, a beautiful use of τ = NIAB.
points: Construction: a coil of N turns on a soft iron core, pivoted between concave pole pieces of a permanent magnet, which make the field radial so the plane of the coil is always parallel to B.
Magnetic torque NIAB is balanced by the spring's restoring torque kφ: kφ = NIAB, so φ = (NAB/k)I. Deflection is proportional to current, giving a linear scale.
Current sensitivity = φ/I = NAB/k (deflection per unit current).
Voltage sensitivity = φ/V = NAB/(kR), where R is the coil resistance.
Doubling N doubles the current sensitivity, but it also doubles R, so the voltage sensitivity stays the same.

topics.title: Converting a galvanometer into an ammeter or voltmeter

learn.hook: A galvanometer is delicate, often going full scale at a few milliamperes. With one well-chosen resistor it becomes a sturdy ammeter or a voltmeter.
points: Ammeter: connect a small shunt resistance S in parallel with the galvanometer (resistance G). Most current bypasses the coil.
Shunt value: S = IgG/(I - Ig), where Ig is the full-scale galvanometer current and I is the required range. The ammeter's resistance is very low, about S.
Voltmeter: connect a large resistance R in series with the galvanometer.
Series value: R = V/Ig - G for a voltmeter of range V. The voltmeter's total resistance is very high.
An ideal ammeter has zero resistance (connected in series); an ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance (connected in parallel).

learn.hook: Sailors on the Indian Ocean trade routes trusted the magnetic compass centuries ago. The same lodestone magic now spins hard disks and runs EV motors.
points: Magnetism is found naturally (lodestone). The Earth itself behaves like a huge magnet whose field points roughly from the geographic south to the geographic north, so a freely suspended magnet settles roughly along the north-south line.
Every magnet has a north and a south pole. Like poles repel, unlike poles attract. Cutting a magnet only gives smaller magnets: isolated poles do not exist.
Iron filings sprinkled around a bar magnet trace a pattern just like that of a current-carrying solenoid.
Magnetic field lines form continuous closed loops (outside from N to S, inside from S to N), never intersect, the tangent gives B, and their crowding shows the field's strength.
Unlike electric field lines, which start and end on charges, magnetic field lines have no start or end.

steps: Each piece develops a new N and S at the cut.
Each piece is a complete, weaker magnet.

topics.title: The bar magnet as a magnetic dipole

learn.hook: Cut a solenoid open in your imagination and you will find a bar magnet inside. Their fields are so alike that we use the same formulas for both.
points: A bar magnet behaves like a solenoid: its magnetism comes from tiny circulating currents in its atoms. Its magnetic moment m points along its axis from S to N.
Far field on the axis: B = (µ₀/4π)(2m/r³), along m.
Far field on the equatorial line: B = -(µ₀/4π)(m/r³), opposite to m.
The magnetic moment can be found from the field it produces, or from the torque it feels in a known field (τ = mB sinθ).
A neutral point is where the magnet's field exactly cancels another field (such as Earth's horizontal field); a compass there shows no preferred direction.

topics.title: A magnetic dipole in a uniform field

learn.hook: Flick a compass needle and it oscillates before settling. Count those oscillations and you can actually compare magnetic fields, an old trick of field scientists.
points: A magnetic dipole in uniform B feels no net force but a torque τ = m × B, magnitude mB sinθ, turning m towards B.
Its potential energy is U = -m·B = -mB cosθ: minimum (stable) at θ = 0, maximum (unstable) at θ = 180°.
A compass needle disturbed from equilibrium oscillates; a stronger field gives a stronger restoring torque and faster oscillations, so oscillation rates can compare fields.
Electrostatic analogue: replace p by m and 1/(4πε₀) by µ₀/4π. Then E-dipole formulas give B-dipole formulas.
Analogy table: torque p × E ↔ m × B; energy -p·E ↔ -m·B; axial field 2p/(4πε₀r³) ↔ µ₀2m/(4πr³).

example.q: A magnet of m = 2 A m² is at 60° to a 0.1 T field. Find the torque and the energy.

learn.reallife: Before electronic magnetometers, surveyors compared the strength of magnetic fields at different places by timing the oscillations of a freely suspended magnet: the faster it oscillated, the stronger the field.

learn.hook: Draw any closed bubble around a magnet, around half a magnet, or around nothing at all. The magnetic flux through it is always exactly zero.
points: Gauss's law for magnetism: the net magnetic flux through any closed surface is zero: ∮B·dS = 0.
Every field line that enters a closed surface also leaves it, because magnetic field lines are closed loops.
This expresses the fact that isolated magnetic poles (monopoles) do not exist; the simplest magnetic source is a dipole.
Contrast: in electrostatics, ∮E·dS = q/ε₀, which can be non-zero because electric charges exist.
Flux through an open surface (not closed) can be non-zero; the law is only about closed surfaces.

example.q: A closed surface surrounds only the north pole end of a bar magnet. What is the net magnetic flux through it?
steps: Field lines leave near the north pole...
...but lines inside the magnet enter the surface from the south side.
Every line that leaves also enters, so the net flux is zero.

learn.hook: Slide an iron rod into a solenoid and the field inside can jump hundreds of times. The material itself joins in. Here is how we describe that.
points: Magnetisation M = net magnetic moment per unit volume (unit A m⁻¹).
Magnetic intensity H is defined by B = µ₀(H + M). In a solenoid, H = nI (from the free current), unit A m⁻¹.
For many materials M = χH, where χ (dimensionless) is the magnetic susceptibility. Then B = µ₀(1 + χ)H = µ₀µrH = µH.
Relative permeability µr = 1 + χ; permeability µ = µ₀µr.
χ is small and negative for diamagnets (bismuth about -1.66 × 10⁻⁵), small and positive for paramagnets (aluminium about 2.3 × 10⁻⁵), and very large and positive for ferromagnets.

learn.hook: A live frog was once levitated in a strong magnet because water in its body is diamagnetic. Even 'non-magnetic' things respond to magnetic fields.
points: Classification by χ: diamagnetic (χ small, negative), paramagnetic (χ small, positive), ferromagnetic (χ large, positive).
Diamagnets are weakly repelled; they move from stronger to weaker field regions, and field lines are slightly pushed out of them. Examples: bismuth, copper, lead, silicon, water, nitrogen at STP.
Superconductors cooled below their critical temperature expel the field completely (χ = -1, µr = 0): the Meissner effect. They are perfect diamagnets.
Paramagnets have atoms with permanent magnetic moments. A field partly aligns them against thermal randomness, so they are weakly attracted, moving from weak to strong field regions.
Examples of paramagnets: aluminium, sodium, calcium, oxygen at STP, copper chloride.

example.q: A bar of bismuth and a bar of aluminium are hung freely between the poles of a strong magnet. How do they settle?
steps: Bismuth is diamagnetic, so it moves away from the strongest field.

example.answer: Bismuth across the field; aluminium along the field

learn.hook: Why is iron so dramatically magnetic while aluminium barely notices a magnet? The answer lies in tiny regions called domains.
points: In ferromagnets (iron, cobalt, nickel, gadolinium), atomic moments line up spontaneously in small regions called domains, each about 1 mm across.
Normally domains point randomly. An applied field grows the domains aligned with it and rotates others, giving a huge M and very large χ; they are strongly attracted.
Hard ferromagnets (alnico, used for permanent magnets) keep their magnetisation; soft ferromagnets (soft iron, used in electromagnets and transformer cores) lose it when the field is removed.
Above a certain temperature, the Curie temperature, a ferromagnet loses its ferromagnetism and becomes paramagnetic.
Problem tips: sign of χ classifies the material; in a non-uniform field, ferromagnets and paramagnets move to stronger fields, diamagnets to weaker fields.

example.q: An iron nail is attracted to a magnet but loses that property after strong heating. Explain.
steps: Iron is ferromagnetic because of aligned domains.
Heating above the Curie temperature destroys the spontaneous alignment.
The nail becomes paramagnetic, only weakly attracted.
example.answer: Heating above the Curie temperature makes iron lose its ferromagnetism

learn.hook: Oersted showed currents make magnetism. Michael Faraday and Joseph Henry asked the reverse: can magnetism make a current? Their answer powers every home in India.
points: Electromagnetic induction: a changing magnetic field (more precisely, a changing magnetic flux) produces an emf and a current in a circuit.
It underlies generators in power plants, transformers, induction cooktops and wireless charging.
Experiment 1: moving a bar magnet towards or away from a coil connected to a galvanometer deflects it. Faster motion gives a larger deflection; no motion, no deflection.
Experiment 2: moving a current-carrying coil towards or away from a second coil induces a current in the second coil.
Experiment 3: with both coils stationary, switching the current in one coil on or off induces a brief current in the other. A steady current induces nothing.

example.q: A magnet is held still inside a coil connected to a galvanometer. What does the galvanometer show? What if the magnet is pulled out quickly?
steps: Stationary magnet: flux through the coil is constant, so no emf.
Pulling it out changes the flux quickly.
example.answer: No deflection when still; a large deflection while it is pulled out quickly

learn.reallife: Every unit of electricity reaching Indian homes from Bhakra Nangal, Tehri or NTPC's coal plants is produced by electromagnetic induction in giant generators.

learn.hook: All of Faraday's experiments had one thing in common: the number of magnetic field lines through the coil was changing. Physicists call it magnetic flux.
points: Faraday's conclusion: an induced emf appears whenever the magnetic flux through a circuit changes.
Magnetic flux through a plane area A in a uniform field: Φ = B·A = BA cosθ, where θ is the angle between B and the normal to the area.
For a non-uniform field: Φ = Σ B·dA (sum over small elements).
Flux is a scalar. SI unit: weber (Wb), 1 Wb = 1 T m².
Flux can be changed in three ways: change B, change the area A, or change the angle θ (rotate the coil).
