learn.hook: The emf you get does not depend on how much flux there is, but on how fast it changes. Faraday turned that idea into a law with one simple equation.
points: Faraday's law: the induced emf equals the negative rate of change of magnetic flux: ε = -dΦ/dt.
For a coil of N turns: ε = -N dΦ/dt. Average emf ε = -NΔΦ/Δt.
Induced current I = ε/R, and the charge that flows Q = NΔΦ/R (independent of how fast the change happens).
Example: pulling a square loop out of a field region changes Φ from BA to 0; the emf depends on how quickly it is removed.
The minus sign expresses Lenz's law: the emf opposes the change.

example.q: A 50-turn coil of area 0.02 m² is perpendicular to a field that drops from 0.5 T to 0.1 T in 0.2 s. Find the average emf.
steps: ΔΦ per turn = ΔB × A = 0.4 × 0.02 = 8 × 10⁻³ Wb

learn.reallife: Electromagnetic flow meters used by Indian water utilities measure flow speed from the emf induced in moving water as it crosses a magnetic field, a direct use of Faraday's law.

items.q: N = 1, ΔΦ = 0.2 Wb in 0.1 s: |ε| (in V)
N = 100, ΔΦ = 0.01 Wb in 0.5 s: |ε| (in V)
N = 10, ΔΦ = 0.3 Wb in 3 s: |ε| (in V)
ε = 6 V, R = 3 Ω: I (in A)
N = 20, ΔΦ = 0.05 Wb, R = 10 Ω: charge (in C)

games.title: Law check
items: Induced emf depends on the rate of change of flux.
ε = -dΦ/dt.
A large but constant flux produces a large emf.
Constant flux gives zero emf.
Doubling the number of turns doubles the induced emf.
ε = -N dΦ/dt.
The total charge that flows depends on how fast the flux is changed.
Q = NΔΦ/R, independent of time.
The minus sign in Faraday's law represents Lenz's law.
The emf opposes the change.

quiz.q: The flux through a single loop changes from 0.06 Wb to 0.02 Wb in 0.1 s. What is the magnitude of the average induced emf (in V)?
quiz.mistake: Uses the final flux instead of the change

quiz.q: A 200-turn coil experiences a flux change of 5 × 10⁻³ Wb per turn in 0.05 s. What is the average emf (in V)?
The flux through a coil is Φ = 3t² + 2t (in Wb, t in s). What is the magnitude of the emf at t = 2 s (in V)?
quiz.explain: |ε| = dΦ/dt = 6t + 2 = 14 V at t = 2 s.

quiz.q: A square loop of side 10 cm and resistance 0.5 Ω lies perpendicular to a 0.5 T field. It is pulled out of the field in 0.1 s. What average current flows (in mA)?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide by the resistance

quiz.q: For the same loop, how much charge flows through it as it is pulled out (in mC)?
quiz.explain: Q = ΔΦ/R = 5 × 10⁻³/0.5 = 10⁻² C = 10 mC, independent of the time taken.

quiz.q: A coil is rotated in a steady field so that its flux changes from a maximum to zero in 0.01 s. If it is rotated twice as fast, the average emf
quiz.explain: Same ΔΦ in half the time doubles ΔΦ/Δt.
steps: Same ΔΦ, but Δt is halved
quiz.mistake: Thinks emf depends only on ΔΦ

quiz.q: The induced emf in a coil does not depend on
options: the rate of change of flux
the area of the coil (for a changing B)
quiz.explain: ε = -N dΦ/dt; resistance affects the current, not the emf.
steps: ε = −N dΦ/dt depends on N and the rate of change of flux
Resistance only affects the current I = ε/R
Answer: the resistance of the coil

quiz.q: Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction is written as
quiz.explain: Induced emf equals minus the rate of change of flux linkage.
steps: Induced emf = minus rate of change of flux linkage
quiz.mistake: Uses flux instead of its rate of change

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Does a stronger magnet always give more induced voltage?'
teach.praise: Chirp! It is the rate of change of flux, times the number of turns, that sets the emf. A still magnet gives nothing!
teach.nudge: Good! What exactly does the emf depend on according to Faraday's law?

revise.summary: Faraday's law states ε = −N dΦ/dt; average emf is NΔΦ/Δt. The induced current is ε/R and the charge moved is NΔΦ/R, independent of how fast the change happens.
traps: Charge does not depend on how quickly the flux changes
Don't forget to multiply by the number of turns N

learn.hook: Drop a strong magnet down a copper pipe and it falls in eerie slow motion. Lenz's law is pushing back.
points: Lenz's law: the induced current flows in a direction that opposes the change in magnetic flux that produced it.
This is a consequence of conservation of energy: you must do work against the opposing force, and that work becomes electrical energy (and heat).
If the induced current helped the change, energy would appear from nothing, which is impossible.
Magnet's N pole approaching a coil: the coil's near face becomes a north pole (repels). N pole moving away: the near face becomes south (attracts).
A loop leaving a field region: the induced current tries to keep the flux, so its own field is in the same direction as the external field.

example.q: A magnet's north pole is pushed towards a coil. Seen from the magnet's side, what is the direction of the induced current?
steps: The coil opposes it by making its near face a north pole.
A north face, seen from outside, has an anticlockwise current.
example.answer: Anticlockwise, as seen from the magnet's side

learn.reallife: Electromagnetic brakes on some metro trains, like Delhi Metro's regenerative systems, use induction: the induced currents oppose the motion, slowing the train and feeding energy back to the grid.

games.title: Lenz logic
items: The induced current always opposes the change in flux.
That is Lenz's law.
Lenz's law follows from conservation of charge.
It follows from conservation of energy.
When a north pole approaches a coil, the near face of the coil becomes a south pole.
It becomes north, to repel.
Work done against the opposing force appears as electrical energy.
Energy is conserved.
A magnet dropped through a copper pipe falls more slowly than in free fall.
Induced currents in the pipe oppose its motion.

quiz.q: A north pole of a magnet moves away from a coil. The face of the coil nearest the magnet becomes a
quiz.explain: The coil opposes the decrease in flux by trying to hold the magnet back.
steps: Moving the N pole away reduces the flux
The coil opposes this by attracting the magnet back
Its near face becomes a south pole
Answer: south pole, attracting the magnet

quiz.q: Lenz's law is a consequence of the law of conservation of
quiz.explain: Opposing the change means work must be done, which becomes electrical energy.
steps: Opposing the change means work must be done against it
That work becomes electrical energy: conservation of energy

quiz.q: A rectangular loop is being pulled out of a region of uniform field pointing into the page. The induced current in the loop flows
options: clockwise, to keep the inward flux
quiz.explain: Inward flux is falling, so the loop makes its own inward field: clockwise current (right-hand rule).
steps: Inward flux falls as the loop leaves the field
The induced current makes its own inward field to keep the flux
Inward field inside a loop needs a clockwise current
Answer: clockwise, to keep the inward flux
quiz.mistake: Opposes the field instead of the change in flux

quiz.q: What would happen if the induced current aided the change in flux instead of opposing it?
options: The current would be very small
Energy would be created from nothing, violating conservation of energy
quiz.explain: A self-reinforcing change would grow without any work input, which is impossible.
steps: If the induced current helped the change, the change would grow by itself
Energy would appear with no work done – impossible
Answer: Energy would be created from nothing, violating conservation of energy
quiz.mistake: Does not see the energy argument

quiz.q: A magnet dropped through a vertical copper tube falls slowly because
options: currents induced in the tube oppose its motion (Lenz's law)
air resistance in the tube is high
quiz.explain: As the magnet falls, the flux through each ring of the tube changes, inducing currents whose magnetic field opposes the magnet's motion (Lenz's law).
steps: The falling magnet changes the flux through each ring of the tube
Induced currents oppose its motion (Lenz's law)
Answer: currents induced in the tube oppose its motion (Lenz's law)

quiz.q: The field through a loop points upward and is increasing. The induced current produces a field that, inside the loop, points
quiz.explain: To oppose the increase of upward flux, the induced field points down.
steps: To oppose the increase, the induced field points downward
quiz.mistake: Points the induced field along the existing field

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Pushing a magnet into a coil requires more effort when the coil's ends are joined than when they are open. Reason (R): With the ends joined, an induced current flows and opposes the motion. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: With an open circuit there is an emf but no current, so no opposing magnetic force.
steps: A: more effort is needed when the ends are joined – true
R: a closed coil carries an induced current that opposes the motion – true
Open ends give emf but no current, so R explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks the emf alone exerts the force

quiz.q: A metal ring is placed around the top of a vertical solenoid. When the current in the solenoid is switched on, the ring
options: jumps up, repelled by the solenoid
quiz.explain: The increasing flux induces a current in the ring that opposes it, so the ring is repelled (the jumping ring experiment).
steps: Switching on gives an increasing flux through the ring
The ring's induced current opposes it, so the ring is repelled
Answer: jumps up, repelled by the solenoid

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why does the induced current always fight the change? Is it just being stubborn?'
teach.praise: Chirp! If it helped, energy would come from nowhere. Opposing the change keeps energy conserved: work in, electricity out!
teach.nudge: Good! Which conservation law would be broken if the induced current helped the change?

revise.summary: Lenz's law says the induced current opposes the change in flux that causes it, a consequence of energy conservation. An approaching N pole makes the near face north (repulsion); a receding one makes it south (attraction).
focus: Statement and energy basis of Lenz's law
Finding the direction of induced current
remember: Induced current opposes the change in flux
Approaching N → near face N; receding N → near face S
Open circuit: emf but no opposing current
traps: The induced field opposes the change, not the field itself
When a loop leaves a field, the induced field is not opposite to the external field; it is along it

learn.hook: Slide a metal rod across two rails in a magnetic field and a voltage appears between its ends, no battery needed. It is the simplest generator possible.
points: A rod of length l moving at speed v perpendicular to a uniform B, on rails forming a loop: area changes at rate lv, so ε = Blv.
Explanation with Lorentz force: each free charge in the rod feels qvB along the rod, pushing charges to one end; the work per unit charge over length l is vBl.
If the circuit has resistance R, current I = Blv/R flows, and the rod feels a retarding force F = BIl = B²l²v/R.
To keep the rod at constant speed, an external force must supply power P = Fv = B²l²v²/R, which equals the electrical power I²R dissipated. Energy is conserved.
The direction of the induced current can be found by Fleming's right-hand rule or by Lenz's law.

example.q: A 0.5 m rod moves at 4 m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a 0.2 T field on rails with R = 2 Ω. Find ε, I and the force needed.

learn.reallife: When a Vande Bharat train speeds along, its steel axle is a long conductor moving through Earth's magnetic field, so a small motional emf exists between the ends of the axle.

games.title: Energy flow in a sliding rod
items: External agent pulls the rod
Rod's motion changes the flux and induces emf Blv
Current I = Blv/R flows
Field exerts a retarding force BIl on the rod
Work done by the agent appears as I²R heat

items.q: B = 1 T, l = 1 m, v = 2 m s⁻¹: ε (in V)
B = 0.5 T, l = 0.2 m, v = 10 m s⁻¹: ε (in V)
ε = 2 V, R = 4 Ω: I (in A)
B = 0.1 T, I = 2 A, l = 0.5 m: force (in N)
Rod moving parallel to B: ε (in V)

quiz.q: A rod of length 0.3 m moves at 5 m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a field of 0.4 T. What emf is induced (in V)?
The same rod (ε = 0.6 V) slides on rails with total resistance 3 Ω. What current flows (in A)?
For that rod (B = 0.4 T, l = 0.3 m, I = 0.2 A), what force is needed to keep it moving at constant speed (in N)?
steps: Retarding force F = BIl; external force must equal it
quiz.mistake: Uses the speed instead of the length

quiz.q: And the mechanical power supplied by the external agent (F = 0.024 N, v = 5 m s⁻¹) is (in W)
quiz.explain: P = Fv = 0.024 × 5 = 0.12 W, which also equals I²R = 0.04 × 3 = 0.12 W.
quiz.mistake: Gives the force instead of power

quiz.q: In terms of the Lorentz force, the emf in a moving rod arises because
options: free charges in the rod feel a force q(v × B) along the rod
the field does work on the charges directly
quiz.explain: This force pushes charges to the ends and does work vBl per unit charge.
steps: Each free charge in the moving rod feels q(v × B) along the rod
This pushes charges to the ends, doing work vBl per unit charge
Answer: free charges in the rod feel a force q(v × B) along the rod
quiz.mistake: Thinks the rod becomes a magnet

quiz.q: If the speed of the rod is doubled, the power needed to keep it moving (resistance fixed) becomes
quiz.explain: P = B²l²v²/R ∝ v².
quiz.mistake: Thinks power is proportional to v

quiz.q: A rod slides on rails in a field. If the circuit is broken (open rails), then
options: an emf exists but no current flows and no retarding force acts
quiz.explain: The emf Blv still appears, but without a closed path there is no current.
steps: Emf Blv still appears across the moving rod
No closed path ⇒ no current ⇒ no BIl force
Answer: an emf exists but no current flows and no retarding force acts
quiz.mistake: Thinks an emf always needs a current

quiz.q: A conducting rod moves parallel to a uniform magnetic field. The induced emf is
quiz.explain: v × B = 0 when v is parallel to B.
steps: v parallel to B ⇒ v × B = 0
quiz.mistake: Applies Blv without checking the direction

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Where does the energy come from when a sliding rod lights a bulb?'
teach.praise: Chirp! The pusher does work against a retarding force BIl, and that work becomes the bulb's energy. Energy conserved!
teach.nudge: Good! What force acts on the rod once current flows, and who has to overcome it?

revise.summary: A rod of length l moving at v perpendicular to B develops ε = Blv, from the Lorentz force on its charges. In a circuit of resistance R, I = Blv/R, the rod feels a retarding force B²l²v/R, and the power needed equals I²R.
focus: Energy conservation in a sliding rod
traps: No emf if v is parallel to B
Power ∝ v², not v

topics.title: Rotating rods, wheels and moving vehicles

learn.hook: An aeroplane's metal wings, a spinning bicycle wheel and a train's axle all cut Earth's magnetic field. Each one is a tiny, unintended generator.
points: A metal rod of length l rotating with angular speed ω about one end, perpendicular to B: different parts move at different speeds (v = ωr). Total ε = ½Bωl².
A metal wheel spinning in an axial field has the same emf between its centre (axle) and rim: ε = ½BωR².
A plane flying horizontally: its wings cut the vertical component of Earth's field, so ε = B_vertical × wingspan × speed.
A train moving on level tracks: its axle (length l) cuts the vertical component, so ε = B_vertical × l × v.
Exercise toolkit: ε = -NdΦ/dt, ε = Blv, ε = ½Bωl², ε = -L dI/dt and ε = -M dI/dt.

example.q: A 0.8 m metal rod rotates at 250 rad s⁻¹ about one end in a field of 0.4 T along its axis of rotation. Find the emf between its ends.

learn.reallife: A passenger jet with a 34 m wingspan flying at 250 m s⁻¹ over north India, where the vertical component of Earth's field is about 3 × 10⁻⁵ T, has roughly 0.26 V across its wingtips. It cannot drive a current because the whole plane moves together.

games.title: Spinning and flying
items: The emf of a rod rotating about one end is ½Bωl².
Average speed along the rod is ωl/2.
A horizontally flying aircraft's wings cut the horizontal component of Earth's field.
It is the vertical component that matters.
Doubling the length of a rotating rod doubles its emf.
ε ∝ l², so it becomes four times.
A spinning bicycle wheel in a magnetic field has an emf between its axle and rim.
Each spoke acts like a rotating rod.
Doubling the angular speed doubles the emf of a rotating rod.
ε ∝ ω.

quiz.q: A 0.5 m rod rotates about one end at 200 rad s⁻¹ in a perpendicular field of 0.4 T. What is the emf between its ends (in V)?
A metal wheel of radius 0.2 m spins at 50 rad s⁻¹ in an axial field of 0.1 T. What is the emf between the axle and the rim (in V)?
A plane with a 40 m wingspan flies horizontally at 250 m s⁻¹ where the vertical component of Earth's field is 4 × 10⁻⁵ T. What is the emf across its wingtips (in V)?
quiz.mistake: Slips by a power of ten

quiz.q: A train's 1.5 m axle moves at 20 m s⁻¹ where the vertical field is 5 × 10⁻⁵ T. What is the emf across the axle (in mV)?
A rotating rod produces 8 V. Its length is halved, keeping B and ω fixed. What is the new emf (in V)?
quiz.mistake: Halves the emf instead of quartering it

quiz.q: Why is the emf of a rod rotating about one end ½Bωl² and not Bωl²?
options: Points along the rod move at speeds from 0 to ωl, so the average speed is ωl/2
Because only half the rod is in the field
Because the rod rotates only half a turn
quiz.explain: Summing B(ωr)dr from 0 to l gives ½Bωl².
steps: A point at distance r moves at v = ωr, from 0 at the pivot to ωl at the tip
Average speed ωl/2, so ε = Bl(ωl/2) = ½Bωl²
Answer: Points along the rod move at speeds from 0 to ωl, so the average speed is ωl/2
quiz.mistake: Uses the tip speed for the whole rod

quiz.q: Which component of Earth's magnetic field causes an emf across the wings of a plane flying horizontally?
quiz.explain: The wings move horizontally, so only the vertical component is perpendicular to both v and the wing.
steps: Wings move horizontally; emf needs B perpendicular to both v and the wing
Only the vertical component satisfies this

quiz.q: A coil of 100 turns has its flux changed by 0.02 Wb per turn in 0.4 s. What is the emf (in V)?

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'A spinning rod's tip moves fastest. Why is its emf ½Bωl²?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Speed grows from zero at the centre to ωl at the tip, so the average is ωl/2, giving ½Bωl². Spin-tastic!
teach.nudge: Good! Do all parts of the rod move at the same speed?

revise.summary: A rod rotating about one end in a perpendicular field develops ε = ½Bωl², as does a spinning wheel between axle and rim. Planes and trains moving horizontally cut Earth's vertical field component, giving ε = B_vertical × l × v.
focus: Emf of a rotating rod or wheel
remember: Plane or train: ε = B_vertical l v
traps: Don't forget the ½ for a rod rotating about one end
For horizontal motion don't use the horizontal component of Earth's field; use the vertical component

learn.hook: Wireless phone chargers, Indian Railways track circuits and every transformer rely on one coil 'talking' to another through changing flux. That link is mutual inductance.
points: For a coil near a current, flux linkage NΦ is proportional to the current. The constant of proportionality is the inductance.
Inductance depends only on the geometry of the coils (turns, size, separation) and the medium (permeability). SI unit: henry (H), 1 H = 1 Wb A⁻¹ = 1 V s A⁻¹.
Mutual inductance: N₁Φ₁ = M₁₂I₂, the flux in coil 1 due to current in coil 2. It can be shown that M₁₂ = M₂₁ = M.
Two long coaxial solenoids (inner radius r₁, length l, turns per metre n₁ and n₂): M = µ₀n₁n₂πr₁²l. With a core of µr, M is multiplied by µr.
Induced emf in one coil due to changing current in the other: ε₁ = -M dI₂/dt.

example.q: Two coils have M = 0.2 H. The current in coil 2 rises from 0 to 5 A in 0.1 s. Find the emf in coil 1.

learn.reallife: Wireless chargers for phones sold in Indian markets put a transmitter coil and a receiver coil close together; the larger their mutual inductance, the better the charging.

games.title: Mutual inductance
items: Mutual inductance depends on the currents flowing in the coils.
It depends only on geometry and medium.
The mutual inductance of coil 1 with respect to coil 2 equals that of coil 2 with respect to coil 1.
M₁₂ = M₂₁.
Moving two coils further apart reduces their mutual inductance.
Less flux links them.
A steady current in one coil induces a steady emf in the other.
Only a changing current induces emf.
Inserting a soft iron core increases mutual inductance.
M is multiplied by µr.

quiz.q: Two coils have a mutual inductance of 1.5 H. The current in one changes at 4 A s⁻¹. What emf is induced in the other (in V)?
A current change from 2 A to 8 A in 0.3 s in coil A induces an average emf of 12 V in coil B. What is M (in H)?

quiz.mistake: Uses the outer radius or forgets π in the area

quiz.q: Which is equivalent to one henry?
quiz.explain: From ε = M dI/dt, M = ε/(dI/dt) has units V/(A s⁻¹) = V s A⁻¹.
steps: Units: V ÷ (A s⁻¹) = V s A⁻¹
quiz.mistake: Gets the time unit upside down

quiz.q: Inductance of a pair of coils depends on
options: the rate of change of current only
their geometry, separation and the medium around them
quiz.explain: M is a geometric and material property, like capacitance.
steps: Inductance, like capacitance, is set by geometry and medium
Turns, size, separation and permeability – not the current
Answer: their geometry, separation and the medium around them

quiz.q: A soft iron core of µr = 500 is put inside a pair of coaxial solenoids with M = 2 mH (in air). What is M now (in H)?
steps: A core multiplies M by µr

quiz.q: Two coils are placed with their planes perpendicular and centres together. Compared with coaxial placement, their mutual inductance is
quiz.explain: The field of one coil hardly threads the other when they are perpendicular.
steps: With perpendicular planes, one coil's field hardly passes through the other
Flux linkage ≈ 0, so M is very small

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Mutual inductance between two coils is the same whichever coil carries the current. Reason (R): M₁₂ = M₂₁ for any pair of coils. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: This reciprocity holds generally, so the induced emf per unit rate of change is the same both ways.
steps: A: M is the same whichever coil carries the current – true
R is exactly this reciprocity, so R explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks the larger coil always has a larger M

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How does a current in one coil create a voltage in another coil that it does not touch?'
teach.praise: Chirp! A changing current in one coil changes the flux through the other, inducing ε = -M dI/dt. No touching needed!
teach.nudge: Good! What must be changing, and what quantity links the two coils?

revise.summary: Flux linkage in one coil is proportional to the current in another: N₁Φ₁ = MI₂, with M₁₂ = M₂₁. M depends on geometry and medium (µ₀n₁n₂πr₁²l for coaxial solenoids), is measured in henry, and gives ε₁ = −M dI₂/dt.
focus: Definition and unit of mutual inductance
remember: 1 H = 1 Wb A⁻¹ = 1 V s A⁻¹
traps: M does not depend on the current
Don't use the outer solenoid's radius; use the inner one's

topics.title: Self-inductance and energy in an inductor

learn.hook: Switch off a large motor and you may see a spark at the switch. The coil fights the sudden drop in its own current with a burst of back emf.
points: Self-inductance: a coil's own flux linkage NΦ = LI. Changing I induces an emf in the same coil: ε = -L dI/dt (back emf).
The back emf opposes any change in current, rising or falling. An inductor plays the role in circuits that mass (inertia) plays in mechanics.
Long solenoid of n turns per metre, area A and length l: L = µ₀n²Al. With a core: L = µrµ₀n²Al.
Energy stored in an inductor: U = ½LI², analogous to kinetic energy ½mv².

Mutual inductance examples: for long coaxial solenoids M = µ₀n₁n₂πr₁²l; for a small loop of radius r₁ at the centre of a large coplanar loop of radius r₂ (r₁ ≪ r₂), the large loop's field µ₀I/(2r₂) is nearly uniform over the small loop, so M = µ₀πr₁²/(2r₂).

example.q: A 0.5 H inductor carries 4 A. Find the stored energy. If the current falls to zero in 0.01 s, what average back emf appears?

learn.reallife: Tube lights in older Indian homes used a choke (an inductor). Its large back emf when the starter opened gave the high voltage spike needed to strike the tube.

games.title: Mechanics and inductors

An inductor of 2 H carries 3 A. How much energy is stored in it (in J)?
quiz.mistake: Forgets the ½ or the square

quiz.q: A solenoid has 1000 turns per metre, cross-section 10⁻³ m² and length 0.5 m. What is its self-inductance (in mH)? (µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷, π = 3.14)
The number of turns per unit length of a solenoid is doubled (same size). Its self-inductance becomes
quiz.explain: L ∝ n².

quiz.q: A small circular loop of radius r₁ lies at the centre of a much larger coplanar circular loop of radius r₂ (r₁ ≪ r₂). What is their mutual inductance?
quiz.explain: A current I in the large loop gives B = µ₀I/(2r₂) at its centre, almost uniform over the small loop. Flux through the small loop = πr₁² × µ₀I/(2r₂), so M = Φ/I = µ₀πr₁²/(2r₂).
steps: Field at centre of large loop: B = µ₀I/(2r₂)
Flux through small loop: Φ = B × πr₁² = µ₀Iπr₁²/(2r₂)

quiz.q: A coil's current rises from 0 to 2 A in 0.05 s, and the average back emf is 8 V. What is L (in H)?

points: Alternating voltage varies sinusoidally with time: v = vm sin ωt, where vm is the peak value and ω = 2πν. Most power supplies in homes and industry are AC.

learn.hook: Put an inductor on AC and something strange happens: the current always reaches its peak a quarter cycle after the voltage. The coil makes the current lag.
points: For v = vm sin ωt across inductance L: i = im sin(ωt - π/2). The current lags the voltage by π/2 (90°).

XL increases with frequency: an inductor lets DC (ω = 0) pass freely but opposes high-frequency AC.
Average power over a cycle in a pure inductor is zero: energy is stored in its field in one quarter cycle and returned in the next.

learn.hook: Radio sets, induction furnaces and the power-factor panels in Indian factories all contain resistors, inductors and capacitors in series. Phasors make them easy.
points: In series, the same current flows through R, L and C. VR is in phase with I, VL leads I by 90°, VC lags I by 90°.
Phasor sum: Vm² = VRm² + (VCm - VLm)², so the impedance is Z = √(R² + (XC - XL)²), with vm = imZ.
Impedance diagram: R along one axis and (XC - XL) at right angles; Z is the hypotenuse.
Phase angle: tanφ = (XC - XL)/R. If XL > XC the circuit is inductive (current lags); if XC > XL it is capacitive (current leads).
Individual voltages VR = IR, VL = IXL, VC = IXC can be larger than the supply voltage, because they are not in phase.

learn.hook: Turn the tuning knob of an old FM radio and one station suddenly comes in loud and clear. You have just made an LCR circuit resonate.
points: Resonance occurs when XL = XC, i.e. ω₀L = 1/(ω₀C), so ω₀ = 1/√(LC) and ν₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)).
At resonance Z = R (minimum) and the current is maximum, im = vm/R. Current and voltage are in phase.

topics.title: Power in AC circuits and power factor

learn.hook: Electricity boards in India charge factories a penalty if their power factor is low. A bank of capacitors can save lakhs of rupees a year.
points: Average power in an AC circuit: P = VI cosφ (V and I are RMS), where φ is the phase difference. cosφ is the power factor.
Pure resistor: φ = 0, cosφ = 1, P = VI. Pure inductor or capacitor: φ = ±90°, cosφ = 0, P = 0. Such current is called wattless current.
Series LCR: cosφ = R/Z. At resonance Z = R, so cosφ = 1 and power is maximum.
A low power factor means a large current for the same useful power, so I²R losses in the lines rise.
Industries add capacitors to cancel the lagging current drawn by motors (inductive loads), raising the power factor towards 1.

example.q: A circuit with R = 60 Ω and Z = 100 Ω is connected to 200 V RMS. Find the power factor and the average power.

learn.reallife: State electricity boards, from Maharashtra's MSEDCL to Tamil Nadu's TANGEDCO, set minimum power factor rules for industrial consumers, which is why factories install capacitor banks.

learn.hook: A phone charger steps 230 V down to about 5 V. The power station steps it up to 400 kV. Both use the same simple device: two coils and an iron core.
points: Principle: mutual induction. An alternating current in the primary coil creates a changing flux in a soft iron core, which induces an emf in the secondary coil.
Ideal transformer: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np, and with no losses VpIp = VsIs, so Ip/Is = Ns/Np.
Step-up transformer: Ns > Np (voltage raised, current lowered). Step-down transformer: Ns < Np.

Energy losses: flux leakage (reduced by winding coils on top of each other), resistance of windings (thick copper wire), eddy currents in the core (laminated core) and hysteresis (soft iron with a narrow loop).
A transformer works only with AC (or changing current); steady DC gives no changing flux.

topics.title: Maxwell's prediction and the first EM waves

learn.hook: Long before Wi-Fi and 5G, a Scottish physicist doing algebra on paper predicted invisible waves that travel at the speed of light. A few decades later, they were found.
points: Faraday showed a changing magnetic field produces an electric field. Maxwell asked: does a changing electric field produce a magnetic field? He concluded it does.
Maxwell's equations then predicted electromagnetic (EM) waves of linked, changing E and B fields, travelling at about 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹: the speed of light. So light itself is an EM wave.
In 1887 Heinrich Hertz produced and detected EM waves in the laboratory, confirming Maxwell.
Jagadish Chandra Bose in Kolkata produced and studied EM waves of much shorter wavelength (about 25 mm to 5 mm).
Guglielmo Marconi transmitted EM waves over many kilometres, opening the era of radio communication.

example.q: Why was Maxwell's calculated speed of EM waves such a big deal?

example.answer: It showed that light is an electromagnetic wave, uniting optics with electricity and magnetism

learn.hook: While a capacitor charges, current flows in the wires but no charge crosses the gap. Yet a compass placed near the gap still feels a magnetic field. Maxwell found the missing current.
points: Ampere's law fails while a capacitor charges: a loop around the wire gives ∮B·dl = µ₀i through a flat surface, but zero through a surface passing between the plates. The results contradict each other.
Between the plates, the electric flux ΦE changes. Maxwell defined displacement current id = ε₀ dΦE/dt.
Ampere-Maxwell law: ∮B·dl = µ₀(ic + ε₀ dΦE/dt) = µ₀(ic + id).
The total current (conduction + displacement) is continuous: in the wires it is all ic, in the gap it is all id, and they are equal.
So a changing electric field produces a magnetic field, just as a changing magnetic field produces an electric field.

topics.title: Maxwell's equations and how EM waves are made

learn.hook: Four short equations describe every electric and magnetic phenomenon, from a static zap to a 5G signal. The fourth one makes waves possible.
points: Maxwell's equations: (1) Gauss's law ∮E·dA = Q/ε₀; (2) Gauss's law for magnetism ∮B·dA = 0; (3) Faraday's law ∮E·dl = -dΦB/dt; (4) Ampere-Maxwell law ∮B·dl = µ₀ic + µ₀ε₀ dΦE/dt. Plus the Lorentz force F = q(E + v × B).
Stationary charges make only E; charges in uniform motion (steady currents) make steady B; but accelerated charges radiate EM waves.
An oscillating charge (for example in an antenna) produces an oscillating E, which produces an oscillating B, and so on: the wave carries away energy at the charge's frequency.
In an EM wave, E and B oscillate perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel: EM waves are transverse.
E, B and the direction of propagation follow the order E × B, giving the direction the wave travels.

example.q: An electron oscillates in an antenna at 100 MHz. What frequency does the radiated wave have, and why?
steps: The fields oscillate at the same frequency as the charge.
So the wave frequency is 100 MHz.
example.answer: 100 MHz, the frequency of the oscillating charge

learn.reallife: The tall masts of Doordarshan and All India Radio have antennas in which electrons are made to oscillate; these accelerated charges launch the waves your TV or radio picks up.

topics.title: Nature and properties of EM waves

learn.hook: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to cross 150 million km of empty space, carrying enough energy to power the solar parks of Rajasthan and to push on solar sails.
points: For a wave travelling along z: Ex = E₀ sin(kz - ωt), By = B₀ sin(kz - ωt), with k = 2π/λ and ω = 2πν. E and B are in phase.

topics.title: EM spectrum: radio, microwave and infrared

learn.hook: Your FM radio, the microwave oven warming leftover biryani and the TV remote are all using light that your eyes cannot see.
points: The EM spectrum is arranged by frequency or wavelength. The regions overlap; there are no sharp boundaries.
Radio waves (λ > 0.1 m): produced by accelerated charges in antennas. AM band 530 kHz to 1710 kHz; FM band 88 MHz to 108 MHz; TV bands from 54 MHz up to 890 MHz; mobile phones use UHF.

Microwaves (0.1 m to 1 mm): produced by special vacuum tubes such as klystrons and magnetrons, and Gunn diodes. Used in radar for aircraft navigation and in microwave ovens, where they heat food by agitating water molecules.

Infrared (1 mm to 700 nm): 'heat waves', given out by hot bodies and vibrating molecules. Used in TV remotes, night vision, physiotherapy heat lamps, and the greenhouse effect warms Earth by trapping IR.
Infrared is detected by thermopiles and bolometers, and many snakes can sense it.

topics.title: EM spectrum: visible, UV, X-rays and gamma rays

learn.hook: Your eyes see only a thin slice of the spectrum, from about 400 nm to 700 nm. Beyond violet lie rays that can disinfect water, image bones and treat cancer.
points: Visible light: about 700 nm (red) to 400 nm (violet). The eye is most sensitive near the middle (yellow-green). Some animals see beyond: honeybees see into the ultraviolet, and snakes can sense infrared.

Ultraviolet (400 nm to 1 nm): produced by the Sun and special lamps. Most solar UV is absorbed by the ozone layer. UV lamps sterilise water and instruments; precise UV lasers are used in LASIK eye surgery. Welders wear special glass goggles to protect eyes from UV.
X-rays (1 nm to 10⁻³ nm): produced by bombarding a metal target with high-energy electrons. Used for medical diagnosis and cancer treatment; overexposure damages tissue.
Gamma rays (below about 10⁻³ nm): produced in nuclear reactions and emitted by radioactive nuclei. Used in medicine to destroy cancer cells.
Higher frequency means higher photon energy, and generally more harmful to living tissue.

points: Radio (> 0.1 m): produced by accelerated charges in aerials; detected by receiver aerials.

topics.title: Light rays and reflection by spherical mirrors

learn.hook: The dentist's small concave mirror and the convex mirror at a hilly hairpin bend in Uttarakhand obey the same two simple laws.
points: Light is electromagnetic radiation; the eye detects wavelengths from about 400 nm to 750 nm. Its speed in vacuum, c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, is a fundamental constant.
Ray optics (geometrical optics): when the wavelength is tiny compared with the objects involved, light can be treated as travelling in straight lines called rays. A bundle of rays is a beam.
Laws of reflection: the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, and the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in one plane.
For a spherical mirror, the normal at any point is along the radius through that point (towards the centre of curvature).

Terms: pole P (centre of the mirror's surface), centre of curvature C, principal axis (line through P and C), aperture (size of the mirror). Paraxial rays are rays close to and nearly parallel to the principal axis.

topics.title: Sign convention and the mirror equation

learn.hook: Mirror problems become simple arithmetic once you agree on one rule for signs. Physicists use the Cartesian sign convention, like a number line placed on the mirror's axis.
points: Cartesian sign convention: all distances are measured from the pole; distances in the direction of incident light are positive, against it negative; heights above the axis are positive, below negative.
With light coming from the left, the object distance u is negative for real objects. Focal length of a concave mirror is negative; of a convex mirror, positive.
Focal length f = R/2 for spherical mirrors (paraxial rays).
Mirror equation: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, derived from similar triangles in a ray diagram.
Magnification m = h'/h = -v/u. Negative m means a real, inverted image; positive m means a virtual, erect image.

example.q: An object is 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 20 cm. Find the image position and magnification.

learn.hook: Where you place an object in front of a concave mirror decides whether you see a huge upright image, an upside-down one, or none at all.

Object at F: image at infinity. Object between F and P: image behind the mirror, virtual, erect, magnified.

learn.hook: A straw in a glass of nimbu pani looks bent at the surface. Light changes speed as it crosses from water to air, and that bends its path.
points: Laws of refraction: the incident ray, refracted ray and normal lie in one plane; and Snell's law: sin i/sin r = n₂₁ (a constant for the pair of media and a given colour).
Refractive index of medium 2 relative to 1: n₂₁ = n₂/n₁ = v₁/v₂. Absolute refractive index n = c/v.
Going from rarer to denser (n₂₁ > 1), the ray bends towards the normal (r < i); from denser to rarer, it bends away from the normal.
Useful relations: n₁₂ = 1/n₂₁, and n₃₂ = n₃₁ × n₁₂.
Typical refractive indices: air 1.0003, water 1.33, crown glass 1.52, diamond 2.42.

learn.reallife: Diamonds cut in Surat, India's diamond capital, sparkle partly because diamond's high refractive index (2.42) bends light strongly.

topics.title: Slabs, apparent depth and total internal reflection

learn.hook: A swimming pool always looks shallower than it is, and on a hot road you see 'water' that is not there. Both tricks come from refraction near a boundary.
points: Glass slab: the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray but shifted sideways (lateral shift), which grows with slab thickness and angle of incidence.
Apparent depth (for near-normal viewing) = real depth/n. A pool 2 m deep in water (n = 4/3) looks 1.5 m deep. The normal shift is d(1 - 1/n).
Going from a denser to a rarer medium, the refracted ray bends away from the normal. At the critical angle ic, the refraction angle is 90°.
Total internal reflection (TIR) happens when light goes from denser to rarer medium AND the angle of incidence exceeds ic. Then all light is reflected.
sin ic = 1/n₂₁ (n of denser relative to rarer). Critical angles: water 48.75°, crown glass about 41°, diamond about 24.4°.

example.q: A coin lies at the bottom of a 12 cm deep beaker of water (n = 4/3). How deep does it appear, and by how much is it raised?
example.answer: Appears 9 cm deep; raised by 3 cm

learn.reallife: Mirages on the Delhi-Jaipur highway in May are caused by refraction and total internal reflection of skylight in hot, less dense air near the road surface.

topics.title: Total internal reflection at work: prisms and optical fibres

learn.hook: The broadband internet reaching Indian villages under BharatNet travels as light, bouncing through glass fibres thinner than a hair.
points: Activity: shine a laser pointer through slightly soapy or milky water in a glass and tilt it; beyond a certain angle the beam reflects completely at the surface. Safety: never look into or point a laser at anyone's eyes, and keep water away from electrical sockets.
Totally reflecting prisms (45°-90°-45° glass prisms, critical angle about 42°) turn rays through 90° (periscopes) or 180° (binoculars), and can invert images without changing size.
They reflect almost 100% of light, better than silvered mirrors.

Optical fibres: a glass or quartz core surrounded by cladding of lower refractive index. Light entering the core undergoes repeated TIR and travels long distances with little loss, even when the fibre bends.
Uses: telecommunication (huge data rates), endoscopy (light pipes to see inside the body), and decorative lamps.

example.q: Why must the cladding of an optical fibre have a lower refractive index than the core?
steps: TIR needs light to go from denser to rarer medium.
The core must be denser than the cladding.
Then rays hitting the boundary beyond ic are totally reflected.
example.answer: So that light in the core is totally internally reflected at the core-cladding boundary

learn.reallife: Gastroenterologists in hospitals across India use endoscopes, bundles of optical fibres, to see inside a patient's stomach without surgery.

topics.title: Refraction at spherical surfaces and the lens maker's formula

learn.hook: An air bubble in a glass paperweight looks bigger or smaller depending on where you look from. A single curved surface can act like a lens.
points: Refraction at a single spherical surface: n₂/v - n₁/u = (n₂ - n₁)/R, using the Cartesian sign convention (light from medium n₁ into n₂).
Applications: the apparent position of an object inside a glass sphere, or of an air bubble seen from outside.

A thin lens has two surfaces; combining the single-surface equation for both gives the lens maker's formula: 1/f = (n₂₁ - 1)(1/R₁ - 1/R₂), where n₂₁ is the lens material's index relative to the surroundings.
For a double convex lens, R₁ is positive and R₂ negative.
A lens in a different medium: its focal length changes because n₂₁ changes. A glass lens (n = 1.5) in water (n = 4/3) has f four times its value in air.

example.q: A double convex lens has R₁ = 20 cm and R₂ = -20 cm, with n = 1.5. Find f.

topics.title: Thin lens formula and power of a lens

learn.hook: An optometrist writes '-1.5 D' on your prescription. That number is the power of a lens, and it tells you exactly how strongly it bends light.
points: Thin lens formula: 1/v - 1/u = 1/f. Magnification m = h'/h = v/u.
Convex (converging) lens: f > 0. Concave (diverging) lens: f < 0. Real images have v > 0 (on the other side); virtual images have v < 0.

Ray diagrams: a convex lens forms real, inverted images when the object is beyond F, and a virtual, erect, magnified image when the object is within F. A concave lens always gives virtual, erect, diminished images.
Power P = 1/f (f in metres). Unit: dioptre (D), 1 D = 1 m⁻¹.
Converging lenses have positive power; diverging lenses have negative power.

learn.hook: Camera and microscope objectives are not single lenses but stacks of them. Adding lenses is as easy as adding their powers.
points: Thin lenses in contact: 1/f = 1/f₁ + 1/f₂ + ...; equivalently P = P₁ + P₂ + ...
Total magnification of a combination: m = m₁m₂m₃...
Lenses at a separation: find the image by the first lens, then use it as the object for the second lens (measuring distances from the second lens).
Combining converging and diverging lenses of different glasses can reduce colour defects in cameras and microscopes.
Problem toolkit: mirror formula, lens formula, lens maker's formula, power, TIR condition, prism relations and instrument magnifications.

learn.hook: A prism bends light twice, once going in and once coming out. There is one special angle where the bending is the least, and it reveals the glass's refractive index.
points: For a triangular prism of angle A: r₁ + r₂ = A, where r₁ and r₂ are the refraction angles inside at the two faces.
Angle of deviation: δ = i + e - A, where i and e are the angles of incidence and emergence.
A graph of δ against i falls to a minimum Dm and then rises again.
At minimum deviation, i = e and r₁ = r₂ = A/2; the ray passes symmetrically. Then n₂₁ = sin[(A + Dm)/2]/sin(A/2).
For a thin prism (small A): δ = (n₂₁ - 1)A.

example.q: A prism of angle 60° gives minimum deviation 30°. Find n.

learn.reallife: Spectrometers in Indian research labs, like those at IIA Bengaluru, use prisms or gratings at minimum deviation to measure the refractive index and to split light into colours.

learn.hook: With a simple lens you can read the tiny print on a medicine strip. With two lenses, a pathologist at a district hospital can see the malaria parasite in a drop of blood.
points: Simple microscope (magnifier): a converging lens with the object within its focal length gives an erect, magnified, virtual image.
Angular magnification: m = 1 + D/f when the image is at the near point (D = 25 cm), and m = D/f when the image is at infinity (relaxed eye).
Compound microscope: an objective of short focal length forms a real, inverted, magnified intermediate image; the eyepiece acts as a simple magnifier on it.
Magnifying power with the final image at infinity: m ≈ (L/fo)(D/fe), where L is the tube length (distance between the second focal point of the objective and the first focal point of the eyepiece).
To get high magnification, both fo and fe should be small.

example.q: A magnifier has f = 5 cm. Find the magnification with the image at the near point (25 cm) and at infinity.
example.answer: 6 at the near point; 5 at infinity

learn.reallife: Pathology labs across India use compound microscopes with 100× oil-immersion objectives and 10× eyepieces, giving a total magnification of about 1000×.

teach.nudge: Good! What do the objective and the eyepiece each do?

revise.summary: A simple microscope gives m = 1 + D/f (image at near point) or D/f (at infinity). A compound microscope's objective forms a real magnified image that the eyepiece magnifies, with m ≈ (L/fo)(D/fe).
remember: Simple: m = 1 + D/f (near point), D/f (infinity); D = 25 cm
traps: Don't use long focal lengths for high m; both fo and fe should be small
The final image of a compound microscope is not erect; it is inverted relative to the object

learn.hook: The Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope near Pune collects faint radio waves from space, while the optical telescopes at Devasthal in Uttarakhand gather faint light from galaxies billions of light years away.
points: Refracting astronomical telescope: an objective of large focal length and large aperture, and an eyepiece of short focal length. The objective forms a real image of a distant object at its focus.
Magnifying power in normal adjustment (final image at infinity): m = fo/fe. Tube length = fo + fe.
A larger objective aperture gathers more light (light-gathering power ∝ area ∝ D²) and gives better resolving power, so fainter and finer details are seen.

Reflecting telescopes (such as the Cassegrain design) use a concave primary mirror and a small convex secondary mirror. Advantages: no chromatic aberration, the mirror can be supported across its back, and large mirrors are cheaper and lighter than large lenses.
The image of a distant object (like the Moon) formed by the objective has size = fo × angle subtended by the object.

example.q: A telescope has fo = 100 cm and fe = 5 cm. Find the magnifying power and the tube length in normal adjustment.

learn.reallife: The 3.6 m Devasthal Optical Telescope near Nainital, India's largest, is a reflecting telescope. Its huge mirror gathers enough light to study faint stars and galaxies.

learn.hook: For over a century, Newton's particle picture of light ruled. Then a thin film of soap and two tiny slits showed that light behaves like waves.
points: Newton favoured a corpuscular (particle) model of light. Huygens (1678) proposed a wave model.

Young's interference experiment (1801) and later Maxwell's electromagnetic theory established the wave nature of light. The wave model also correctly predicts that light travels slower in water than in air.
Ray optics is the limit of wave optics when the wavelength is very small compared with the size of obstacles and apertures.
A wavefront is a surface of constant phase. A point source gives spherical wavefronts; a line source gives cylindrical ones; far from any source, small portions are plane wavefronts.
Rays are perpendicular to wavefronts, and energy travels along the rays, perpendicular to the wavefront.

example.q: What shape of wavefront reaches Earth from a distant star, and why?
steps: A star is a point source, so its wavefronts are spherical.
Its distance is enormous, so the sphere's radius is huge.
A small part of a huge sphere is practically flat.

learn.reallife: The rainbow colours you see in a soap bubble or an oil film on a wet Mumbai road during the monsoon are evidence of light's wave nature through interference.

steps: Huygens proposed the wave theory in 1678

revise.summary: Newton favoured particles, but Huygens proposed waves, and Young's interference (1801) and Maxwell's theory established light as a wave. A wavefront is a surface of constant phase, spherical near a point source and plane far away, with rays perpendicular to it.
remember: Point source → spherical; line source → cylindrical; distant → plane
Rays ⟂ wavefronts; light slower in water
traps: Huygens, not Newton, proposed the wave theory
Energy flows perpendicular to, not along, wavefronts

learn.hook: Drop pebbles in a still pond: each ripple spreads in circles. Huygens imagined every point on a wave doing exactly that.
points: Huygens principle: every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets that spread out at the wave speed. The new wavefront is the forward envelope (common tangent) of these wavelets.
The backward wave is ignored; a fuller theory shows that the amplitude of the backwave is zero, so the wave only goes forward.
Reflection by Huygens construction: comparing two triangles formed by the incident and reflected wavefronts proves that i = r.

Wavefronts through optical elements: a plane wave through a thin prism is tilted; through a convex lens it becomes a converging spherical wave; after reflection from a concave mirror it becomes a spherical wave converging to the focus.
Optical paths: all rays from a point to its image take the same time (equal optical path), which is why lenses work.

example.q: Explain using Huygens principle why a plane wave stays plane as it travels in a uniform medium.
steps: Each point on the plane wavefront sends out spherical wavelets.
After time t, all have radius vt.
Their forward common tangent is a plane parallel to the original.
example.answer: The envelope of equal wavelets is a parallel plane, so the wave stays plane

learn.reallife: Ultrasound scanners in Indian hospitals shape their beams using arrays of tiny sources, an engineering application of Huygens' idea that a wavefront is built from many secondary wavelets.

quiz.q: In Huygens' principle, the secondary wavelets in a uniform medium travel with

So they travel at the same speed as the wave

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A lens forms an image because all rays from an object point reach the image point in equal times. Reason (R): Light travels slower in glass, so the thicker central part of a convex lens delays the central rays. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false

quiz.explain: Extra glass in the middle compensates for the shorter geometrical path, equalising travel times.
steps: A: rays from an object point reach the image in equal times – true
R: thicker glass at the centre delays central rays – true

Answer: Both A and R are true, and R explains A

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How did Huygens explain how a wave moves forward?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Every point on a wavefront sends out secondary wavelets; their forward envelope is the new wavefront. Ripple power!
teach.nudge: Good! What does each point on a wavefront do in Huygens' picture?

revise.summary: Huygens principle: each point of a wavefront emits secondary wavelets and the new wavefront is their forward envelope. It explains reflection (i = r) and how prisms, lenses and mirrors reshape wavefronts.
remember: New wavefront = forward envelope of wavelets
Convex lens / concave mirror: plane → converging spherical
traps: Secondary wavelets do not travel faster or slower; they move at the same speed as the wave
Image formation needs equal optical paths, not equal geometric paths

learn.hook: Imagine a marching band walking from a road onto sand at an angle. The band members who hit the sand first slow down, and the whole row turns. Light does the same.
points: Huygens construction for refraction: while one end of the wavefront travels v₁τ in medium 1, the wavelet from the other end travels v₂τ in medium 2. Comparing triangles gives sin i/sin r = v₁/v₂ = n₂/n₁ (Snell's law).
Entering a denser medium (v₂ < v₁): the ray bends towards the normal.
Frequency stays the same across the boundary; speed and wavelength change: λ₂/λ₁ = v₂/v₁, so λ in medium = λ₀/n.
Going into a rarer medium (v₂ > v₁): the ray bends away from the normal. When sin i = v₁/v₂, r = 90°; beyond this critical angle, no refracted wavefront forms, giving total internal reflection.
Example: in glass of n = 1.5, light of vacuum wavelength 600 nm has λ = 400 nm and speed 2 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

example.q: Yellow light of wavelength 589 nm in air enters water (n = 1.33). Find its frequency, speed and wavelength in water.

learn.reallife: Fishermen in Kerala aim their spears below where a fish appears, because light from the fish refracts at the water surface, bending as its speed changes.

That is Snell's law.

Only from denser to rarer.
In a denser medium, light travels more slowly.
v = c/n.

learn.hook: Two speakers playing the same note can make spots of silence in a room. Light waves can do the same, if their sources are perfectly in step.
points: Coherent sources keep a constant phase difference; incoherent sources have a phase difference that changes randomly and rapidly.
Two coherent waves of equal intensity I₀ meeting with phase difference φ give resultant intensity I = 4I₀ cos²(φ/2).
Constructive interference (bright, I = 4I₀) for path difference nλ (φ = 2nπ); destructive (dark, I = 0) for path difference (n + ½)λ (φ = (2n + 1)π).
For incoherent sources, the cos² term averages to ½, so the intensities simply add: I = 2I₀. No fringes are seen.
Interference can be demonstrated with water waves: two dippers moving up and down together in a ripple tank produce lines of calm and agitated water.

revise.summary: Coherent sources keep a constant phase difference. Two coherent waves of intensity I₀ give I = 4I₀cos²(φ/2): bright for path difference nλ and dark for (n + ½)λ; incoherent sources just add to 2I₀.

learn.hook: Thomas Young needed two light sources perfectly in step. His trick was simple and brilliant: split the light from one source using two pinholes.
points: Two independent sources are incoherent. Young used light from a single source passing through two narrow slits S₁ and S₂, which then act as coherent sources.
For slits separated by d, screen at distance D (D ≫ d), the path difference at a point at height x on the screen is S₂P - S₁P ≈ xd/D.
Bright fringes at x = nλD/d (n = 0, ±1, ±2...); dark fringes at x = (n + ½)λD/d.
Fringe width (distance between consecutive bright or dark fringes): β = λD/d. The fringes are equally spaced.
The central fringe (x = 0, zero path difference) is always bright.

revise.summary: In Young's experiment two slits lit by one source act as coherent sources. At height x the path difference is xd/D, so bright fringes lie at nλD/d and dark fringes at (n + ½)λD/d, with equal fringe width β = λD/d.

learn.hook: Swap red light for blue, dunk the apparatus in water, or move the screen back: each tweak stretches or squeezes the fringes in a predictable way.
points: β = λD/d: β increases with λ and D, and decreases with d.
Immersing the apparatus in a liquid of refractive index n reduces λ to λ/n, so β becomes β/n.
With white light, the central fringe is white, and the others are coloured: violet (shorter λ) fringes lie nearer the centre, red ones farther out. Only a few fringes are visible.
Energy is redistributed in interference: it is not destroyed at dark fringes but moved to bright ones.
Fringe shift problems: λ can be found from measured fringe width or from the change in position of a given fringe when D or λ changes.

learn.hook: Look at a street light through a narrow gap between two fingers on a dark night. You will see faint bright and dark bands: light bending round the edges.
points: Diffraction is the bending of light around the edges of obstacles or apertures whose size is comparable to the wavelength.
A single slit of width a gives a broad central maximum with weaker secondary maxima and minima on either side.
Minima occur at a sinθ = nλ (n = ±1, ±2, ...); secondary maxima lie roughly at θ ≈ (n + ½)λ/a, with intensity falling quickly.
Angular width of the central maximum = 2λ/a; on a screen at distance D its linear width = 2λD/a. The central maximum is twice as wide as each secondary maximum.
Narrower slits give wider diffraction patterns.

learn.reallife: The coloured patterns you see in the tiny tracks of a CD or DVD lying in an Indian home, or in a peacock's feathers, involve diffraction and interference of light.

learn.hook: Both interference and diffraction give bright and dark bands. A careful look at the band widths and brightness tells you which one you are seeing.
points: Interference (two slits): fringes of equal width β = λD/d and (ideally) equal intensity.
Diffraction (single slit): a central maximum twice as wide as the others, with intensity falling rapidly for higher orders.
Interference comes from superposition of waves from two separate (coherent) sources; diffraction from superposition of wavelets from different parts of one wavefront.

learn.hook: Tilt your head while wearing polarising sunglasses and look at an LCD screen: it can go dark. Light has a hidden direction, and polaroids can reveal it.
points: Polarisation shows that light is a transverse wave. Analogy: a wave on a string passes through a vertical slit only if the string vibrates vertically.
Unpolarised light (sunlight, bulbs) has its electric field vibrating in all directions perpendicular to the direction of travel, changing randomly.
Plane (linearly) polarised light has its electric field vibrating in one direction only.
A polaroid transmits only the component of E along its pass axis. Unpolarised light of intensity I₀ through one polaroid becomes polarised with intensity I₀/2, whatever the polaroid's orientation.
A second polaroid (the analyser) rotated in front of the first changes the intensity: maximum when the axes are parallel, zero when crossed.

example.q: Unpolarised light of intensity 80 W m⁻² passes through a polaroid. What is the transmitted intensity, and does it change if the polaroid is rotated?
steps: A polaroid transmits half of unpolarised light.
Rotating it does not change this, because unpolarised light has no preferred direction.

learn.reallife: Polarising sunglasses popular with drivers on Indian highways cut glare from wet roads and car bonnets, because the reflected glare is partly polarised.

topics.title: Malus' law and uses of polaroids

learn.hook: 3D movies in Indian multiplexes send two polarised images at once, one for each eye. Your 3D glasses use polaroids to separate them.

chapters.title: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter

topics.title: Electrons and how they escape metals

learn.hook: The solar panels on rooftops from Gujarat to Tamil Nadu rely on light knocking electrons free. To understand them, we start with the electron itself.
points: J.J. Thomson (1897), studying cathode rays in discharge tubes, showed they are streams of negatively charged particles, electrons, and measured their charge-to-mass ratio e/m. Millikan's oil-drop experiment measured the charge e (about 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C).
This raised a deep question: do light and matter have both wave and particle character?
Free electrons in a metal cannot normally leave its surface; they are held by the attraction of the positive ions. Extra energy is needed to pull them out.

Work function φ₀: the minimum energy needed to free an electron from a metal surface, usually given in eV (1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J). It depends on the metal and its surface; caesium has a low value (about 2.14 eV) and platinum a high one (about 5.65 eV).
Ways to supply this energy: thermionic emission (heating), field emission (very strong electric field, about 10⁸ V m⁻¹), and photoelectric emission (light of suitable frequency).

learn.reallife: Old television picture tubes and the X-ray tubes at Indian diagnostic centres use thermionic emission: a heated filament boils off electrons.

learn.hook: In 1887, Heinrich Hertz noticed that sparks jumped more easily when ultraviolet light shone on his metal electrodes. He had stumbled on the photoelectric effect.
points: Hertz (1887): ultraviolet light falling on the spark gap made high-voltage sparks pass more easily.
Hallwachs and Lenard (1886–1902): UV light on a zinc plate releases negatively charged particles (electrons). A negatively charged zinc plate loses its charge, while a neutral one becomes positive.
There is a threshold frequency ν₀: below it no electrons are emitted, however intense the light.
Alkali metals (lithium, sodium, potassium, caesium, rubidium) emit electrons even with visible light; zinc, cadmium and magnesium need ultraviolet. Such materials are called photosensitive.

Experimental set-up: an evacuated glass tube with a photosensitive plate (emitter, cathode C) and a collector (anode A), a variable potential difference between them, a microammeter, and a monochromatic light source through a quartz window.

example.q: A neutral zinc plate on an electroscope is exposed to UV light. What happens to the leaves and why?

example.answer: The leaves diverge because the plate becomes positively charged

learn.reallife: The automatic doors at Indian metro stations and malls once used photocells: light falling on a photosensitive surface gave a current, and blocking the beam changed it.

learn.hook: Turn up the brightness of the light in a photocell and the current rises. But the fastest electrons do not get any faster. That surprised everyone.
points: For a frequency above threshold, the photocurrent (and number of electrons emitted per second) is directly proportional to the intensity of light.
As the anode's positive potential increases, the photocurrent rises and then levels off: the saturation current, when all emitted electrons are collected.
Making the anode negative reduces the current; at the stopping potential V₀ (cut-off), even the fastest electrons are stopped and the current becomes zero. Then Kmax = eV₀.
For a given frequency, the stopping potential is the same for all intensities; only the saturation current changes.
Emission is instantaneous: electrons come out within about 10⁻⁹ s of the light being switched on, even for very dim light.

topics.title: Effect of frequency, and why wave theory failed

learn.hook: Classical physics said: make the light bright enough and electrons will fly out at any colour. Experiments said no. Something had to give.
points: For a given metal, the stopping potential V₀ increases linearly with the frequency ν of the incident light.
A graph of V₀ against ν is a straight line cutting the ν-axis at the threshold frequency ν₀. Below ν₀, no emission.
For different metals, the lines are parallel (the same slope, h/e), but they have different threshold frequencies.
Wave theory predicted that Kmax should increase with intensity, since a brighter wave carries more energy. Experiment shows Kmax depends only on frequency.
Wave theory also could not explain the existence of a threshold frequency or why emission is instantaneous (it predicted a long delay for dim light while energy builds up).

example.q: For a metal, V₀ = 0 at ν = 5 × 10¹⁴ Hz and V₀ = 2 V at ν = 10 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Find the slope h/e.
example.answer: 4 × 10⁻¹⁵ V s (so h = slope × e ≈ 6.4 × 10⁻³⁴ J s from these data, close to the accepted 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)

learn.reallife: Physicists at India's Raman Research Institute in Bengaluru and elsewhere still teach this experiment as the moment classical physics broke and quantum physics was born.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why couldn't the wave picture of light explain the photoelectric effect?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Wave theory couldn't explain the threshold frequency, why Kmax ignores intensity, or why emission is instant. Time for photons!

learn.hook: In 1905 Einstein proposed that light comes in packets of energy. One equation then explained everything the wave theory could not, and won him the Nobel Prize.
points: Light consists of quanta (photons), each of energy E = hν, where h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s (Planck's constant). One photon is absorbed by one electron.
Einstein's equation: Kmax = hν - φ₀ = eV₀.
Threshold frequency ν₀ = φ₀/h; threshold wavelength λ₀ = c/ν₀ = hc/φ₀. No emission if ν < ν₀ (or λ > λ₀).

This explains: threshold (photon energy must exceed φ₀); Kmax rising linearly with ν; intensity affecting only the number of photons (and so the current); instantaneous emission (one photon, one electron, no waiting).
Millikan's careful experiments verified the equation; the slope h/e of the V₀-ν graph gave a value of h close to Planck's.

learn.reallife: Solar cells on ISRO's satellites and on Indian rooftops work on the photon idea: each absorbed photon with enough energy frees one electron to drive a current.

topics.title: Photons in collisions and photon counting

learn.hook: A 1 W LED glows with billions of billions of photons every second. Counting them is as simple as dividing power by the energy of one photon.
points: Photons are electrically neutral, so they are not deflected by electric or magnetic fields.
In photon-particle collisions (such as photon-electron collisions), total energy and total momentum are conserved, but the number of photons need not be: photons can be absorbed or created.
Number of photons emitted per second by a source of power P at wavelength λ: n = P/(hν) = Pλ/(hc).
Photon energy E = hν = hc/λ; photon momentum p = h/λ.
For a fixed power, shorter-wavelength (higher-energy) light means fewer photons per second.

learn.hook: If light waves can act like particles, can particles act like waves? A young Louis de Broglie said yes in 1924, and electrons proved him right.
points: de Broglie hypothesis: a moving particle of momentum p has an associated wavelength λ = h/p = h/(mv).
For everyday objects λ is unimaginably tiny (a cricket ball's is about 10⁻³⁴ m), so no wave effects are seen. For electrons, λ is comparable to atomic spacings, so wave effects are clear.
In terms of kinetic energy K: λ = h/√(2mK). For an electron accelerated through V volts: λ = h/√(2meV) ≈ 1.227/√V nm.
Wave-particle duality: both radiation and matter show wave and particle aspects, but not both in the same measurement.
Electron microscopes use the very short de Broglie wavelength of fast electrons to resolve details far smaller than optical microscopes can.

Comparing particles: at the same speed, λ ∝ 1/m; at the same kinetic energy, λ ∝ 1/√m; for the same accelerating voltage V and charge q, λ ∝ 1/√(mq).

topics.title: Thomson's model and the gold foil experiment

learn.hook: Imagine firing cannon shells at a sheet of tissue paper and seeing a few bounce straight back. That was Rutherford's astonishment at the gold foil results.
points: Atoms are electrically neutral, and each element gives a characteristic spectrum. A good atomic model must explain both structure and spectra.
Thomson's 'plum pudding' model (1898): positive charge spread uniformly through the atom, with electrons embedded like seeds in a watermelon. It could not explain large-angle scattering.

Geiger-Marsden experiment (1911, suggested by Rutherford): a beam of alpha particles was aimed at a very thin gold foil; scattered particles were detected by flashes on a zinc sulphide (ZnS) screen viewed through a microscope.
Observations: most alpha particles passed straight through; a few were deflected through large angles; a very few (about 1 in 8000) were turned back by more than 90°.
Conclusion: the atom's positive charge and nearly all its mass are concentrated in a tiny central nucleus, about 10⁴ to 10⁵ times smaller than the atom; most of the atom is empty space.

topics.title: Impact parameter and distance of closest approach

learn.hook: How close can an alpha particle get to a gold nucleus before it is turned back? Energy conservation gives a surprisingly simple estimate of nuclear size.
points: The path of an alpha particle near a nucleus depends on its impact parameter b: the perpendicular distance of its initial line of motion from the nucleus.
Small b (nearly head-on) gives large scattering angles; b = 0 means the particle turns back (scattering through 180°). Large b gives little deflection.
In a head-on approach, the alpha particle stops momentarily at the distance of closest approach d, where all its kinetic energy has become electric potential energy.
K = (1/4πε₀)(2e)(Ze)/d, so d = (1/4πε₀)(2Ze²)/K.
d gives an upper limit for the nuclear size; for gold and alpha energies of a few MeV, d is a few × 10⁻¹⁴ m.

topics.title: Electron orbits and the trouble with Rutherford's model

learn.hook: Rutherford's atom was a mini solar system. But classical physics predicted that it should collapse in a split second. Clearly, something was missing.
points: In Rutherford's planetary model, the electron orbits the nucleus with the Coulomb attraction providing centripetal force: mv²/r = e²/(4πε₀r²).
Kinetic energy K = e²/(8πε₀r), potential energy U = -e²/(4πε₀r), total energy E = K + U = -e²/(8πε₀r).
The total energy is negative, meaning the electron is bound to the nucleus. Energy must be supplied to free it.
Limitation 1: an orbiting electron accelerates, and by classical EM theory it should radiate energy continuously, spiralling into the nucleus. Atoms would be unstable.
Limitation 2: a spiralling electron would emit a continuous range of frequencies, but atoms emit sharp line spectra.

example.q: For a hydrogen electron orbit, K = 13.6 eV. Find U and the total energy E.

learn.reallife: Fluorescent tube lights and sodium-vapour street lamps along Indian highways glow in definite colours, line spectra that Rutherford's model could not explain.

learn.hook: Astronomers know what distant stars are made of without ever visiting them. Each element leaves a unique barcode of light.
points: When a gas or vapour is excited (for example by an electric discharge or heating), it emits light only at certain wavelengths: an emission line spectrum of bright lines on a dark background.
Each element has its own characteristic set of lines.
When white light passes through a cool gas, the gas absorbs light at the same wavelengths it would emit, giving dark lines on a continuous background: an absorption spectrum.
The emission and absorption lines of an element appear at the same wavelengths.
Because spectra are unique, they act as fingerprints for identifying elements in labs, in industry and in stars (helium was first discovered in the Sun's spectrum).

example.q: Sodium vapour gives a bright yellow emission line near 589 nm. Where will a dark line appear if white light passes through cool sodium vapour?
steps: Absorption lines lie at the same wavelengths as emission lines.

learn.reallife: Forensic and food-testing labs in India, including those under FSSAI, use atomic absorption spectroscopy to detect metals like lead in food and water.

learn.hook: In 1913 Niels Bohr rescued the nuclear atom by making three bold rules. They broke classical physics but matched the hydrogen spectrum beautifully.
points: Postulate 1: electrons revolve in certain stable orbits (stationary states) without radiating energy.
Postulate 2: in these orbits, angular momentum is quantised: L = mvr = nh/2π, where n = 1, 2, 3, ... is the principal quantum number.
Postulate 3: an electron emits or absorbs a photon only when it jumps between orbits: hν = Ei - Ef.
Radius of the nth orbit: rn = n²h²ε₀/(πme²), so rn ∝ n². The smallest, the Bohr radius, is a₀ ≈ 5.3 × 10⁻¹¹ m (0.53 Å).
Speed of the electron in the nth orbit vn ∝ 1/n; in the first orbit v₁ ≈ 2.2 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ (about c/137).

example.q: Find the radius of the third orbit of hydrogen and the electron's speed there, compared with the first orbit.
example.answer: r₃ = 4.77 Å; speed is one third of the first orbit's

learn.reallife: Astronomers at Indian observatories such as Hanle and Devasthal still label hydrogen lines by Bohr's quantum numbers (for example the n = 3 to n = 2 line), and his model is the first quantum atom taught in every CBSE Class 12 classroom.

learn.hook: An electron in hydrogen lives on an energy staircase. The bottom step is at -13.6 eV, and the steps crowd together as they climb towards zero.
points: Energy of the nth level of hydrogen: En = -13.6/n² eV. E₁ = -13.6 eV, E₂ = -3.4 eV, E₃ = -1.51 eV, E₄ = -0.85 eV, ... up to E∞ = 0.
n = 1 is the ground state; n ≥ 2 are excited states. The energy level diagram shows levels getting closer together as n increases.
Ionisation energy of hydrogen from the ground state = 13.6 eV. Excitation energy from n = 1 to n = 2 = 10.2 eV.
Energy needed to ionise from level n is 13.6/n² eV. Above E = 0 the electron is free and can have any (continuous) energy.
The Franck-Hertz experiment (1914) gave direct evidence for discrete energy levels: electrons colliding with mercury atoms lost energy only in definite amounts.

learn.reallife: The plasma physicists at the Institute for Plasma Research, Gandhinagar, study hydrogen at temperatures where atoms are ionised, i.e. electrons have been pushed above the E = 0 level.

learn.hook: Every line in the hydrogen spectrum is an electron jumping down the energy staircase and throwing off a photon whose energy matches the drop.
points: A spectral line arises when an electron jumps from a higher level ni to a lower level nf, emitting a photon of energy hν = Ei - Ef.

Absorption lines correspond to the same energy differences in reverse (nf → ni upward).
A transition from n = 3 to n = 2 gives a red line near 656 nm; transitions ending on n = 1 give ultraviolet lines.
Handy shortcut: λ (in nm) = 1240/ΔE (in eV).

topics.title: Bohr's orbits as matter waves, and limits of the model

learn.hook: Why should angular momentum come in multiples of h/2π? A decade after Bohr, de Broglie's matter waves gave a beautiful answer.
points: de Broglie's explanation: an electron in a Bohr orbit is a standing wave, like a vibrating string closed into a circle.
For a stable standing wave, the circumference must hold a whole number of wavelengths: 2πr = nλ.
With λ = h/(mv): 2πr = nh/(mv), so mvr = nh/2π, exactly Bohr's quantisation condition.

Limitations of Bohr's model: it works only for hydrogen-like atoms (one electron, such as He⁺ and Li²⁺); it cannot explain the relative intensities of spectral lines or the spectra of many-electron atoms.
Problem toolkit: rn ∝ n², vn ∝ 1/n, En ∝ -1/n²; number of spectral lines from level n down to ground state = n(n - 1)/2.

example.q: An electron in hydrogen is excited to n = 4. How many different spectral lines can be emitted as it returns to the ground state?

learn.reallife: Guitar and sitar strings vibrate only at frequencies that fit whole numbers of half-wavelengths on them; de Broglie pictured electrons in atoms the same way.

learn.hook: If an atom were the size of a cricket stadium, its nucleus would be a small marble at the centre spot, yet the marble would hold almost all of the stadium's mass.
points: The nucleus is about 10⁴ times smaller than the atom (radius ~10⁻¹⁴ m versus ~10⁻¹⁰ m), but contains more than 99.9% of the atom's mass.
Questions for this chapter: what is a nucleus made of, how big and heavy is it, what holds it together, and how can nuclear energy be released?
Atomic mass unit: 1 u = 1/12 of the mass of one carbon-12 atom = 1.660539 × 10⁻²⁷ kg (≈ 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg).
Atomic masses are measured precisely with a mass spectrometer.
Non-integral atomic masses arise from isotopes. Chlorine is about 75.4% ³⁵Cl and 24.6% ³⁷Cl, so its average atomic mass is about 35.47 u.

learn.hook: For years, physicists puzzled over why nuclei were heavier than their protons alone. In 1932, James Chadwick found the missing piece: the neutron.
points: The proton is the nucleus of a hydrogen atom, with charge +e and mass about 1.00728 u.

The neutron was discovered by James Chadwick (1932) when beryllium was bombarded with alpha particles and gave out neutral, penetrating radiation. Its mass is about 1.00866 u, slightly more than the proton's.
A nucleus has Z protons (atomic number) and N neutrons; the mass number A = Z + N is the total number of nucleons. It is written ᴬ_Z X (for example ¹⁹⁷₇₉Au).
Isotopes: same Z, different A (¹H, ²H, ³H). Isobars: same A, different Z (³H and ³He). Isotones: same N, different Z (¹⁹⁸₈₀Hg and ¹⁹⁷₇₉Au, both N = 118).
A free neutron is unstable (it decays into a proton, an electron and an antineutrino), but it is stable inside many nuclei.

learn.hook: A teaspoon of nuclear matter would weigh about a billion tonnes. That is the density of a nucleus, and of a neutron star.
points: From scattering experiments: nuclear radius R = R₀A^(1/3), with R₀ ≈ 1.2 fm (1 fm = 10⁻¹⁵ m).
So nuclear volume (4/3)πR³ ∝ A: each nucleon occupies about the same volume.
Nuclear density = mass/volume ≈ (A × 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷)/((4/3)πR₀³A) is independent of A, about 2.3 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.
This is roughly 10¹⁴ times the density of ordinary matter (water is 10³ kg m⁻³).
Neutron stars are giant 'nuclei' with roughly this density.

learn.hook: Weigh a helium nucleus precisely and you find it lighter than the two protons and two neutrons that make it. The 'missing' mass became binding energy.
points: Einstein's mass-energy equivalence: E = mc². Mass and energy can be converted into each other.
1 u of mass is equivalent to 931.5 MeV of energy. One gram of matter is equivalent to 10⁻³ × (3 × 10⁸)² = 9 × 10¹³ J.
Mass defect: ΔM = [Zmp + (A - Z)mn] - M, the difference between the total mass of free nucleons and the mass M of the nucleus.
Binding energy Eb = ΔMc²: the energy needed to break the nucleus completely into separate protons and neutrons (or the energy released when they come together).
With atomic masses: ΔM = Z m(¹H) + N mn - m(atom), since electron masses cancel.
